s2_metadata.abstract: Temperature dependence of vibrational modes in semiconductors depends on lattice thermal expansion and anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering. Evaluating the two contributions from experimental data is not straightforward, especially for epitaxial layers that present mechanical deformation and anisotropic lattice expansion. In this work, a temperature-dependent Raman study in epitaxial Ge and Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$ layers is presented. A model is introduced for the Raman mode energy shift as a function of temperature, comprising thermal expansion of the strained lattice and anharmonic corrections. With support of x-ray diffraction, the model is calibrated on experimental data of epitaxial Ge grown on Si and Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$ grown on Ge/Si, finding that the main difference between bulk and epitaxial layers is related to the anisotropic lattice expansion. The phonon anharmonicity and other parameters do not depend on dislocation defect density (in the range $7\cdot 10^6$ - $4\cdot 10^8$ cm$^{-2}$) nor on alloy composition in the range 5-14 at.%. The strain-shift coefficient for the main model of Ge and for the Ge-Ge vibrational mode of Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$ is weakly dependent on temperature and is around -500 cm$^{-1}$. In Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$, the composition-shift coefficient amounts to -100 cm$^{-1}$, independent of temperature and strain.

s2_metadata.abstract: Epitaxial growth of III-V semiconductors on Si is a promising route for silicon photonics. Threading dislocations and the residual thermal stress generated during growth are expected to affect the thermal conductivity of the III-V semiconductors, which is crucial for efficient heat dissipation from photonic devices built on this platform. In this work, we combine a non-contact laser-induced transient thermal grating technique with ab initio phonon simulations to investigate the in-plane thermal transport of epitaxial GaAs-based buffer layers on Si, employed in the fabrication of III-V quantum dot lasers. Surprisingly, we find a significant reduction of the in-plane thermal conductivity of GaAs, up to 19%, as a result of a small in-plane biaxial stress of 250 MPa. Using ab initio phonon calculations, we attribute this effect to the enhancement of phonon-phonon scattering caused by the in-plane biaxial stress, which breaks the cubic crystal symmetry of GaAs. Our results indicate the importance of eliminating the residual thermal stress in the epitaxial III-V layers on Si to avoid the reduction of thermal conductivity and facilitate heat dissipation. Additionally, our results showcase potential means of effectively controlling thermal conductivity of solids with external strain/stress.

s2_metadata.abstract: α- and κ-Ga2O3 are promising candidates for high-performance devices such as high-power electronics, but the low thermal conductivity (TC) severely hinders its application. Strain inevitably exists in practical Ga2O3-based devices due to the mismatch of lattice structure and thermal expansion brought by heteroepitaxial growth, and it significantly influences the thermal properties of α- and κ-Ga2O3. By employing first-principles calculations and the phonon Boltzmann transport equation, we have studied the TC at the induced strain and optimized strain axis in free states and 16 different strain states. The TC at the induced strain and optimized strain axis generally decreases with increasing strain. Under −4% XZ-axes biaxial compressive strain, the kzz of α-Ga2O3 can increase to ∼1.7 times its original value, while under −2% XY-axes biaxial compressive strain, the kxx of κ-Ga2O3 can increase to 2.8 times its original value. The improvement of thermal transport properties is attributed to the increase in phonon group velocity and relaxation time caused by the phonon hardening and decrease in three-phonon scattering channels, respectively. However, we observed an exception: under +4% X-axis tensile strain, kyy of α-Ga2O3 increased by 1.1 times. Moreover, atomic bond analysis revealed that under XY-direction strain, the ICOHP values for α-Ga2O3 are −3.94 eV (at −4% strain), −3.76 eV (unstrained state), and −3.63 eV (+4% strain). This discovery elucidates the origin of phonon hardening under compressive strain, indicating that strengthened bonds enhance phonon transport. This study provides essential insights into the mechanisms of α- and κ-Ga2O3 TC under different strains.

s2_metadata.abstract: Thanks to recent breakthroughs in their epitaxy compatible with industrial standard, (Si)GeSn alloys are now emerging as material platform for monolithic integration of next-generation electronics, optoelectronics, thermoelectrics, and photonics. In order to support the rapid evolution of the (Si)GeSn material system, different advanced characterization methods have to be developed to investigate its many interesting physical properties. This work provides an overview of Raman spectroscopy investigation of binary GeSn and ternary SiGeSn alloys. After reviewing the fundamental principles of Raman spectroscopy, the typical features of (Si)GeSn alloy Raman spectra are introduced. These features are then attributed to vibrational modes of atom pairs, high-order scattering, or disorder-induced scattering. The discussion also covers the details of polarization-resolved Raman spectroscopy applied specifically to the group-IV alloys case, with a focus on probing the local atomic ordering. Different applications of the Raman spectroscopy to the (Si)GeSn material system are covered. Initially, micro-Raman measurements are complemented by ancillary techniques, such as x-ray diffraction. This allows the spatially resolved composition and strain of the investigated epitaxial alloys to be determined based on calibrated coefficients of vibrational mode shifts. Raman hyperspectral imaging, along with its integration with numerical simulations for strain mapping in microstructures and devices, is also presented. Subsequently, temperature-dependent Raman spectra are employed to investigate the crystal anharmonicity and the lattice expansion, with a detailed analysis of the multiple-phonon scattering coefficients, that are then compared with data present in the literature. The temperature dependence of Raman modes is also used to develop Raman thermometry to measure lattice thermal conductivity, in view of the recently proposed use of these materials in integrated opto–thermo-electronic devices. In summary, Raman spectroscopy is demonstrated as an essential tool for metrology and physical insight of the technologically relevant and complex SiGeSn ternary alloy system.

s2_metadata.abstract: Strained Si technology is important for engineering field-effect transistors (FETs) [1,2]. There are two types of the strained Si technologies. One is so-called global strained Si technology. Another is so-called local strained Si technology. The former is the technology of using a strained Si substrate which has a several-dozen-nanometers-thick strained Si layer at the top of the substrate [3-5]. The strained Si layer is obtained by growing Si on SiGe, therefore, large tensile strain with biaxial isotropy can be induced in Si. The isotropic biaxial tensile strain in Si allows for performance improvements for both of nand ptype FETs. Homogeneous strain distribution can be obtained under the critical thickness of the strained Si layer [6].

s2_metadata.abstract: Two-dimensional group IV transition-metal dichalcogenides have encouraging thermoelectric applications since their electronic and lattice properties can be manipulated with strain. In this paper, we report the thermoelectric parameters such as electrical conductivities, Seebeck coefficients, electrical relaxation times, and the mode dependent contributions to the lattice thermal conductivity of ZrX 2 ( X = S , Se , Te) from first-principles methods. Our calculations indicate that due to tensile strain, the power factor increases while simultaneously decreasing the lattice thermal conductivity, thus enhancing the thermoelectric figure of merit. Tensile strain widens the bandgap, which corresponds to a higher power factor. The lattice thermal conductivity decreases due to the stiffening of the out-of-plane phonon modes, thus reducing the anharmonic scattering lifetimes and increasing the thermoelectric figure-of-merit.Two-dimensional group IV transition-metal dichalcogenides have encouraging thermoelectric applications since their electronic and lattice properties can be manipulated with strain. s2_metadata.abstract: While phonon topology in crystalline solids has been extensively studied, its influence on thermal transport-especially in nanostructures-remains elusive. Here, by combining first-principles-based machine learning potentials with the phonon Boltzmann transport equation and molecular dynamics simulations, we systematically investigate the role of topological surface phonons in the in-plane thermal transport of semiconductor thin films (Si, 4H -SiC, and c-BN). These topological surface phonons, originating from nontrivial acoustic phonon nodal lines, not only serve as key scattering channels for dominant acoustic phonons but also contribute substantially to the overall thermal conductivity. Remarkably, for these thin semiconductor films below 10 nm this contribution can be as large as over 30% of the in-plane thermal conductivity at 300 K, and the largest absolute contribution can reach 82 W/m-K, highlighting their significant role in nanoscale thermal transport in semiconductors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both temperature and biaxial strain provide effective means to modulate this contribution. Our work establishes a direct link between topological surface phonons and nanoscale thermal transport, offering the first quantitative assessment of their role and paving the way for topology-enabled thermal management in semiconductors.

s2_metadata.abstract: The phonon dispersion, density of states, Gr\"{u}neisen parameters, and the lattice thermal conductivity of single- and multi-layered boron nitride were calculated using first-principles methods. For the bulk {\it h}-BN we also report the two-phonon density of states. We also present simple analytical solutions to the acoustic vibrational mode-dependent lattice thermal conductivity. Moreover, computations based on the elaborate Callaway-Klemens and the real space super cell methods are presented to calculate the sample length and temperature dependent lattice thermal conductivity of single- and multi-layered hexagonal boron nitride which shows good agreement with experimental data.

s2_metadata.abstract: Anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering serves a critical role in heat conduction in solids. Previous studies have identified many selection rules for possible phonon-phonon scattering channels imposed by phonon energy and momentum conservation conditions and crystal symmetry. However, the crystal-symmetry-based selection rules have mostly been ad hoc so far in selected materials, and a general formalism that can summarize known selection rules and lead to new ones in any given crystal is still lacking. In this work, we apply a general formalism for symmetry-based scattering selection rules based on the group theory to anharmonic phonon-phonon scatterings, which can reproduce known selection rules and guide the discovery of new selection rules between phonon branches imposed by the crystal symmetry. We apply this formalism to analyze the phonon-phonon scattering selection rules imposed by the in-plane symmetry of graphene, and demonstrate the significant impact of symmetry-breaking strain on the lattice thermal conductivity. Our work quantifies the critical influence of the crystal symmetry on the lattice thermal conductivity in solids and suggests routes to engineer heat conduction by tuning the crystal symmetry.

s2_metadata.abstract: The aggressive downscaling of complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) technology to the sub-21-nm technology node is facing great challenges. Innovative technologies such as metal gate/high-k dielectric integration, source/drain engineering, mobility enhancement technology, new device architectures, and enhanced quasiballistic transport channels serve as possible solutions for nanoscaled CMOS. Among them, mobility enhancement technology is one of the most promising solutions for improving device performance. Technologies such as global and process-induced strain technology, hybrid-orientation channels, and new high-mobility channels are thoroughly discussed from the perspective of technological innovation and achievement. Uniaxial strain is superior to biaxial strain in extending metal–oxide–semiconductor field-effect transistor (MOSFET) scaling for various reasons. Typical uniaxial technologies, such as embedded or raised SiGe or SiC source/drains, Ge pre-amorphization source/drain extension technology, the stress memorization technique (SMT), and tensile or comprehensive capping layers, stress liners, and contact etch-stop layers (CESLs) are discussed in detail. The initial integration of these technologies and the associated reliability issues are also addressed. The hybrid-orientation channel is challenging due to the complicated process flow and the generation of defects. Applying new high-mobility channels is an attractive method for increasing carrier mobility; however, it is also challenging due to the introduction of new material systems. New processes with new substrates either based on hybrid orientation or composed of group III–V semiconductors must be simplified, and costs should be reduced. Different mobility enhancement technologies will have to be combined to boost device performance, but they must be compatible with each other. The high mobility offered by mobility enhancement technologies makes these technologies promising and an active area of device research down to the 21-nm technology node and beyond.

s2_metadata.abstract: Hole mobility and velocity are extracted from scaled strained-Si0.45Ge0.55 channel p-MOSFETs on insulator. Devices have been fabricated with sub-100-nm gate lengths, demonstrating hole mobility and velocity enhancements in strained- Si0.45Ge0.55 channel devices relative to Si. The effective hole mobility is extracted utilizing the dR/dL method. A hole mobility enhancement is observed relative to Si hole universal mobility for short-channel devices with gate lengths ranging from 65 to 150 nm. Hole velocities extracted using several different methods are compared. The hole velocity of strained-SiGe p-MOSFETs is enhanced over comparable Si control devices. The hole velocity enhancements extracted are on the order of 30%. Ballistic velocity simulations suggest that the addition of (110) uniaxial compressive strain to Si0.45Ge0.55 can result in a more substantial increase in velocity relative to relaxed Si.

s2_metadata.abstract: On the basis of detailed first-principles calculations the anisotropic thermoelectric transport properties of biaxially strained silicon were studied with the focus on a possible enhancement of the power factor. Electron as well as hole doping was examined in a broad doping and temperature range. In the low temperature and low doping regime an enhancement of the power factor was obtained for compressive and tensile strain in the electron-doped case, and for compressive strain in the hole-doped case. In the thermoelectrically more important high temperature and high doping regime a slight enhancement of the power factor was only found for the hole-doped case under small biaxial tensile strain. The results are discussed in terms of band structure effects. An analytical model is presented to understand the fact that the thermopower decreases if degenerate bands are energetically lifted due to a strain-induced redistribution of states.

s2_metadata.abstract: Germanium (Ge) has been identified as a good candidate among semiconductor‐based materials for quantum applications. One of the main reasons lies in the long coherence time of spins of localized holes, its ability to host superconducting pairing correlations, and compatibility with complementary metal‐oxide‐semiconductor (CMOS) technology. Recent studies reveal how the growth of strained germanium quantum wells (QWs) embedded in silicon‐germanium (SiGe) barriers is crucial to enhance charges' mobility in this system. In this work, a study is presented of the distribution of in‐plane and out‐of‐plane strain in germanium quantum wells embedded in Si1 − xGex barriers in order to engineer strain in the quantum well, thus tuning the charge mobility therein for quantum computing purposes. Therefore, experimental techniques such as Raman spectroscopy, transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and geometric phase analysis (GPA) are combined with Schrödinger–Poisson solver simulations in order to find the optimal quantum well thickness and silicon (Si) content in the Si1 − xGex barriers to enhance and control electrical properties in Ge/SiGe planar heterostructures.

extracted_data.name_full: Biaxially strained silicon thin film (atomically smooth, reconstructed surfaces)
extracted_data.brief_description: Computational study of in-plane lattice thermal conductivity of Si thin films (various surface orientations) under applied biaxial strain (-3% to +3%) using first-principles-trained machine-learning potentials combined with PBTE and HNEMD; includes mode-resolved group velocities, lifetimes, and weighted phase space and quantifies contributions from low-frequency topological surface phonons.
extracted_data.citation_title: Topological surface phonons modulate thermal transport in semiconductor thin films
extracted_data.material_system: Silicon thin films (Si (111) a-type and Si (001) a-/b-type thin films), atomically thin films / membranes (thicknesses studied ≲ 10 nm; key results at ≈3 nm)
extracted_data.growth_and_microstructure: Not an experimental growth study — computational thin-film models; surfaces relaxed and in many cases show 2×1 reconstructions (Si (001) a- and b-type and Si (111) surfaces). Films described as atomically smooth but with reconstructed surface geometries; no substrate/buffer stack or dislocation network reported.
extracted_data.crystal_orientation: Si (111) a-type and Si (001) a-/b-type thin films; transport reported as in-plane (no cross-plane kappa reported).
extracted_data.strain_type_and_state: Biaxial tensile/compressive strain applied computationally (biaxial in-plane strain); treated as coherent/pseudomorphic imposed lattice distortion in simulation (no explicit substrate relaxation or misfit dislocations modeled).
extracted_data.strain_magnitude: Applied biaxial strain varied from -3% (compressive) to +3% (tensile); strain applied in-plane in simulations (no XRD/Raman experimental determination — purely computational).
extracted_data.film_thickness_and_geometry: Thicknesses studied from ≈1 nm up to ≈5 nm in BTE results (and up to ≲10 nm in HNEMD); key strain-dependent results shown for ≈3 nm-thick films; periodic in-plane, free surface cross-plane with surface reconstructions.
extracted_data.temperature_range: Temperature-dependent calculations from 200 K to 600 K (in-plane kappa and topological-surface-mode contributions extracted); strain-dependence shown at room temperature (300 K) in figure captions.
extracted_data.measurement_or_simulation_method: Theory/simulation: phonon Boltzmann transport equation (ShengBTE) using harmonic and third-order IFCs from neuroevolution potentials (NEPs) trained to DFT (PBEsol for Si); homogeneous nonequilibrium MD (HNEMD) with GPUMD used for larger/thicker cells; Green's-function open-boundary calculations for surface LDOS; mode classification via eigenvector amplitude criterion.
extracted_data.reported_kappa_in_plane: Reported in relative terms and ranges: Si (001) a-/b-type: a 1.4 nm film has in-plane kappa up to ~20% of bulk Si (bulk taken as ~150 W/m-K), which corresponds to ~30 W/m-K (implied by the paper's numbers). Si (111): a 1.7 nm film achieves ~12% of bulk (~18 W/m-K implied). Thickness-dependent curves shown in Fig. 5; absolute numbers for each thickness are plotted in figures (BTE and HNEMD results). Additionally, mode-resolved contributions: topological-surface-state-dominated phonons contribute ≥20% (Si (001) a/b for t < 3.02 nm) and ≥30% (Si (111) for t < 4.5 nm) of the in-plane kappa at 300 K (absolute values implied from the plotted kappa).
extracted_data.unstrained_or_reference_case: Unstrained computational thin films (0% biaxial strain) and bulk Si used as references; bulk Si thermal conductivity value quoted as ~150 W/m-K (Glassbrenner & Slack) used for percentage comparisons. Comparisons are between strained films, unstrained films, and bulk values.
extracted_data.observed_strain_effect_summary: Biaxial strain modulates the in-plane lattice thermal conductivity and the contribution of low-frequency topological surface phonons: for Si (111) thin films the contribution of topological-surface-dominated phonons first increases and then decreases as biaxial strain varies from -3% to +3% (nonmonotonic behavior); overall in-plane kappa is tunable by biaxial strain (strain-dependent results shown at room temperature). The authors attribute the strain sensitivity primarily to strain-driven changes in surface reconstruction and corresponding modulation of low-frequency surface phonon states rather than to a simple bulk-stiffening/softening picture.
extracted_data.phonon_dispersion_or_velocity_changes: Paper reports that low-frequency topological surface phonon states exist and often have large group velocities; group velocities and dispersions were computed (mode-resolved) for ≈3 nm films (Fig. 4). Under biaxial strain the manuscript states low-frequency topological surface states are modulated (especially for Si where surface reconstructions are sensitive to strain), but no numeric per-mode velocity changes under strain are provided in the main text; changes are described qualitatively (modulation/redistribution and possible lifting of degeneracies due to reconstruction).
extracted_data.anharmonicity_metrics: Mode-resolved weighted phase space (WPS) and mode lifetimes (from three-phonon scattering via third-order IFCs) are computed and reported (Fig. 4). The paper does not report explicit Grüneisen parameters or tabulated third-order constants in the main text; anharmonic scattering strength is characterized via WPS and lifetimes. Strain-related changes to WPS/anharmonicity are discussed qualitatively (strain modulates the surface-state spectrum and thus scattering channels) but quantitative Grüneisen trends are not provided.
extracted_data.phonon_lifetimes_or_mfp: Mode-resolved lifetimes are reported: topological-surface-state-dominated phonons show relatively long lifetimes compared to other modes (Fig. 4, lifetime panels). Lifetimes increase at lower temperatures (supporting the observed temperature dependence). The paper provides mode-resolved lifetimes and uses them to compute k contributions, but does not provide an explicit tabulated MFP distribution under different strains in the main text.
extracted_data.scattering_mechanisms_considered: Intrinsic three-phonon scattering (Normal and Umklapp) included via third-order IFCs in PBTE; surface/topological-surface phonons act as additional scattering channels for long-wavelength bulk-like acoustic phonons (discussed and quantified via mode coupling); boundary/thickness (finite-thickness) effects are inherently present in the thin-film calculations; isotope, alloy, dislocation, and electron-phonon scattering channels are not included or emphasized for these Si thin-film simulations.
extracted_data.interfaces_and_boundary_conditions: Cross-plane free surfaces with surface reconstructions are modeled (open boundary in cross-plane for LDOS via Green's function; periodic in-plane in BTE/HNEMD). No explicit interface thermal boundary resistance (TBR) models or substrate interfaces are included; simulations assume freestanding thin-film geometries (no substrate or capping layers).
extracted_data.theoretical_model_and_key_parameters: Phonon BTE solved with ShengBTE using harmonic and third-order IFCs from neuroevolution potentials (NEPs) trained to DFT; DFT functional: PBEsol for Si (for training data); NEP active learning strategy used. HNEMD calculations via GPUMD used to cross-check BTE and extend to thicker films. Mode-classification threshold: a mode is called 'topological surface state-dominated' if vibrational amplitude of surface atoms > 1.2× that of bulk atoms in the eigenvector. Strain implemented by applying uniform in-plane biaxial lattice strain (−3% to +3%) and relaxing atom positions/surface reconstructions accordingly; calculations recompute IFCs under each strain state.
extracted_data.mode_resolved_or_spectral_results: Mode-resolved group velocities, lifetimes, and WPS presented for ≈3 nm Si films (Fig. 4). Mode classification separates bulk-dominated and topological-surface-dominated modes; cumulative contributions show that low-frequency topological surface modes carry a substantial fraction (≥30% for Si (111) at small thickness) of in-plane kappa. Spectral decomposition (frequency-resolved contributions) and identification of dominant low-frequency modes are provided (figures and main text).
extracted_data.confounding_factors_and_limitations: Authors note results provide a lower bound for contributions of low-frequency topological surface states because only modes predominantly characterized by these states (amplitude ratio>1.2) were counted; surface reconstructions complicate direct comparison with Green's-function ideal-surface results; calculations are computational (no explicit substrate or experimental strain implementation), so effects of realistic epitaxy, misfit dislocations, interface roughness, and extrinsic defects are not included; BTE approach becomes computationally prohibitive for thicker films and HNEMD is used there. These factors limit direct applicability to experimentally grown strained films where relaxation/misfit defects may occur.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Fig. 4: mode-resolved group velocities, lifetimes, and WPS for ≈3 nm Si (111) (and other materials); Fig. 5: thickness-dependent lattice thermal conductivities (BTE and HNEMD) and absolute/relative contributions of topological-surface-state-dominated phonons; Fig. 6(c): strain-dependent room-temperature in-plane lattice thermal conductivity and topological-surface contributions for Si (111) a-type (strain range -3% to +3%); Fig. 3: LDOS and identification of surface vs bulk modes; Supporting Information contains many additional dispersion/LDOS/phonon-data figures (e.g., Figs. S5–S13, S19–S23) referenced in the main text.

extracted_data.material_system: Biaxially strained bulk-like silicon (simulated bulk; face-centered tetragonal 8-atom cell; in-plane biaxial strain imposed in simulation).
extracted_data.growth_and_microstructure: Not an experimental film — simulated bulk; no growth; strain imposed by changing in-plane lattice constant while keeping cell volume constant.
extracted_data.crystal_orientation: In-plane biaxial strain (authors change in-plane lattice parameter Δa/a0); transport resolved into in-plane and cross-plane components (orientation of cross-plane corresponds to direction perpendicular to imposed in-plane strain).
extracted_data.strain_type_and_state: In-plane biaxial tensile and compressive strain (simulated, coherent/pseudomorphic deformation in the unit cell).
extracted_data.strain_magnitude: Strain range discussed up to about ±3% for analytical limits; specific low-strain values highlighted (e.g., Δa/a0 = 0.2%–0.6% for optimized PF in holes); many results shown for small strains (few tenths of a percent) and up to ~1% in figures.
extracted_data.temperature_range: Electronic transport/κ_el results presented for 100 K (low-T) and 900 K (high-T); κ_el vs doping shown for 300 K, 500 K and 900 K (inset of Fig.9); discussion references lattice κ_ph values across 300–1200 K from literature.
extracted_data.measurement_or_simulation_method: DFT (GGA-PBE) with fully relativistic norm-conserving pseudopotentials (Quantum ESPRESSO); temperature-dependent scissor operator applied to gap; electronic transport from linearized Boltzmann equation in relaxation time approximation (RTA) using a constant, strain-independent τ; κ_el computed from transport distribution (L^(n) integrals).
extracted_data.reported_kappa_in_plane: Electronic thermal conductivity κ_el was computed and plotted (inset of Fig.9) for 300, 500, 900 K as a function of doping; explicit numeric tabulation of κ_el is not given in the text except the statement that at high doping (>1e20 cm^-3) and 900 K κ_el can be ~1–3 W/m·K (i.e., electronic contribution may be ~25–50% of total for very low κ_ph cases). The lattice thermal conductivity κ_ph is not computed in this work.
extracted_data.unstrained_or_reference_case: Unstrained bulk Si used as reference for electronic transport; for ZT estimates the authors used literature lattice κ_ph values (e.g., 36 W/m·K for bulk Si at 900 K).
extracted_data.observed_strain_effect_summary: The authors did not compute lattice thermal conductivity under strain. They note (from literature) that tensile strain can reduce lattice κ by up to ~15% in bulk silicon and silicon thin films, but this was not included in their ZT estimates. For electronic transport, strain strongly modifies σ and S (via valley splitting and band-structure redistribution) but σ and S changes largely compensate so no substantial enhancement of electronic powerfactor is achieved.
extracted_data.phonon_dispersion_or_velocity_changes: No phonon dispersion or phonon group velocity calculations for lattice thermal conductivity are presented in this work. The paper examines electronic band-structure (valley splitting Δ2/Δ4) and electronic group velocities for electrons, not phonons.
extracted_data.scattering_mechanisms_considered: For electronic transport: intervalley (optical phonon) scattering and its reduction under strain are discussed qualitatively; τ is taken constant and strain-independent. For lattice thermal conductivity (literature discussion): ion (dopant) scattering, boundary scattering (nanostructuring), and interface scattering (superlattices) are cited as mechanisms that reduce κ_ph, but no phonon-scattering calculations are done here.
extracted_data.interfaces_and_boundary_conditions: Not applicable to the DFT bulk simulation; when estimating ZT the authors adopt literature κ_ph values for bulk, nanostructured bulk, and superlattice and explicitly note the assumption of 'no degradation of electronic transport' in the superlattice case.
extracted_data.theoretical_model_and_key_parameters: DFT GGA-PBE; temperature-dependent scissor operator for band gap (U_GGA = 0.57 eV and Varshni temperature dependence); Boltzmann transport in RTA with constant τ (τ assumed independent of k, energy and strain); Fermi-surface integrals done with extended tetrahedron method on dense k-grids (~13950 irreducible k-points). Relaxation time magnitudes referenced from experiment (unstrained): electrons 15–150 fs, holes 6–65 fs.
extracted_data.mode_resolved_or_spectral_results: No mode-resolved lattice (phonon) contributions presented. Electronic transport analysis discusses contributions from different conduction valleys (Δ2 vs Δ4) and valence bands (HH/LH/SO) to anisotropic electronic transport.
extracted_data.confounding_factors_and_limitations: Authors explicitly state they did not compute lattice κ under strain and instead used literature κ_ph values for ZT estimates; constant and strain-independent relaxation time τ is a major approximation; neglect of strain-induced changes to κ_ph in ZT estimates is a limitation (they note literature suggests strain can change κ_ph up to ~15%); no microstructural defects, dislocations, or interface roughness are modeled.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Fig.4–6: anisotropic electronic transport (σ, S, PF) vs biaxial strain for electrons and holes; Fig.7–8: optimized PF vs strain; Fig.9: doping-dependent ZT estimates using literature κ_ph values (inset of Fig.9 shows computed κ_el vs doping for 300/500/900 K).

extracted_data.growth_and_microstructure: Referenced as an epitaxial superlattice; the present work assumes a 15 nm period and 'no degradation of electronic transport' when using the κ_ph value, but does not detail growth method.
extracted_data.strain_type_and_state: Implicitly coherently strained superlattice in referenced experiments, but this paper does not detail strain state; treated as a low-κ phonon-scattering structure.
extracted_data.film_thickness_and_geometry: Superlattice period assumed 15 nm for the ZT estimate; no film thickness given.
extracted_data.temperature_range: Value adopted in this paper for ZT estimate at 300 K (dotted-line ZT in Fig.9).
extracted_data.measurement_or_simulation_method: Experiment (reference [11] cited); exact measurement technique not specified in this paper (reference gives experimental thermal conductivity).
extracted_data.reported_kappa_in_plane: κ_ph = 1.9 W/m·K (value taken from ref. [11] and used in ZT estimate in this paper). The paper does not specify whether this is in-plane or cross-plane component.
extracted_data.unstrained_or_reference_case: Used as a low-κ reference for comparison to bulk Si and nanostructured bulk Si in ZT estimates.
extracted_data.observed_strain_effect_summary: The superlattice exhibits strongly reduced lattice thermal conductivity (used value 1.9 W/m·K). The present paper assumes this low κ_ph can be realized without degrading electronic transport (assumption stated explicitly).
extracted_data.phonon_dispersion_or_velocity_changes: Not analyzed in this paper; reduction in κ_ph attributed in general to interface scattering and zone-folding effects in superlattices in the literature.
extracted_data.scattering_mechanisms_considered: Implicitly interface scattering and superlattice phonon scattering are the dominant mechanisms reducing κ_ph in superlattices; this paper does not present explicit scattering calculations.
extracted_data.interfaces_and_boundary_conditions: Superlattice interfaces and associated phonon-interface scattering are the implied origin of low κ_ph; the authors note they assumed no electronic transport degradation across interfaces when using the κ_ph value.
extracted_data.confounding_factors_and_limitations: Paper uses literature κ_ph value and assumes no degradation of electronic transport — an explicit caveat. No separation of in-plane vs cross-plane κ provided in this work.
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Fig.9 (dotted line) uses κ_ph = 1.9 W/m·K for Si/Ge superlattice in ZT estimate (300 K).

extracted_data.name_full: Epitaxial Si1−xGex alloy thin films grown on (001) Si substrates
extracted_data.brief_description: Experimental study measuring through-thickness thermal conductivity of epitaxial Si1−xGex alloy thin films (39–427 nm) via TDTR and analyzing reductions relative to bulk using a Debye/RTA model that includes Umklapp, alloy and boundary scattering; authors conclude boundary scattering of long-wavelength phonons (size effects) dominates reductions in thin films.
extracted_data.citation_title: Experimental Investigation of Size Effects on the Thermal Conductivity of Silicon-Germanium Alloy Thin Films
extracted_data.material_system: Si1-xGex alloy thin films (epitaxial films on Si (001) substrates); planar films on bulk Si substrate
extracted_data.composition_x: x = 0.20 (Si0.8Ge0.2) measured as thickness series; additional composition-series samples: x = 0.345 (34.5% Ge) and x = 0.45 (45.0% Ge). Paper also discusses behavior for 0.2 < x < 0.8 in analysis.
extracted_data.substrate_and_buffer: 100 mm (001)-oriented single-crystalline silicon substrates; no graded relaxed buffer or virtual substrate reported.
extracted_data.growth_and_microstructure: Epitaxial growth by metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD); film stoichiometry by Rutherford backscattering, thickness by x-ray reflectivity and cross-sectional TEM, surface roughness by AFM. Plan-view TEM shows dislocation density increases with film thickness; defects present especially in thicker films. No quantitative interface roughness or coherent-layer claim is given.
extracted_data.crystal_orientation: Substrate orientation (001) specified. Thermal transport measured in cross-plane (through-thickness) direction by TDTR. No in-plane transport direction or in-plane k reported.
extracted_data.strain_type_and_state: Not explicitly reported as 'strained' or 'coherent' in the paper. Films are epitaxial on Si(001) and thus may experience biaxial lattice mismatch strain for some thicknesses/compositions, but TEM shows increasing dislocation density with thickness indicating partial relaxation/relaxed state for thicker films; authors do not claim fully coherent pseudomorphic films.
extracted_data.strain_magnitude: Not reported; no quantitative in-plane or out-of-plane strain values, mismatch percentages, or c/a distortions provided.
extracted_data.film_thickness_and_geometry: Measured film thicknesses (thickness series, Si0.8Ge0.2): 39 ± 0.9 nm, 88 ± 1.8 nm, 202 ± 2.1 nm, 427 ± 2.1 nm. Composition series: 88 ± 1.8 nm (20.0% Ge), 135 ± 10.4 nm (34.5% Ge), 126 ± 10.1 nm (45.0% Ge). Films coated with an Al transducer for TDTR.
extracted_data.temperature_range: Thermal conductivities measured at room temperature and temperature-dependent measurements performed from 141 K to 300 K for selected samples.
extracted_data.measurement_or_simulation_method: Experimental: Time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR), double-color pump-probe with Al transducer; Al thickness confirmed by picosecond acoustics. Modeling/analysis: analytic Debye, dispersionless relaxation-time approximation (RTA) model (Eq. (1) in paper) with Matthiessen's rule combining Umklapp (τ_U), alloy (τ_α), and boundary (τ_b) scattering. Model constants A, B, C taken from Ref. [31]; cutoff frequency ω_c = 2π v / a with lattice constant a from Vegard's law.
extracted_data.reported_kappa_in_plane: Not reported (no separate in-plane thermal conductivity measurements provided).
extracted_data.reported_kappa_cross_plane: Reported effective through-thickness thermal conductivity (W m^-1 K^-1) measured by TDTR: For 20.0% Ge thickness series: 39 nm: 1.83 ± 0.09 W m^-1 K^-1; 88 nm: 2.17 ± 0.10 W m^-1 K^-1; 202 nm: 2.69 ± 0.10 W m^-1 K^-1; 427 nm: 2.84 ± 0.18 W m^-1 K^-1. Composition-series: 88 nm (20.0% Ge): 2.17 ± 0.10 W m^-1 K^-1; 135 nm (34.5% Ge): 1.68 ± 0.30 W m^-1 K^-1; 126 nm (45.0% Ge): 1.79 ± 0.39 W m^-1 K^-1. Values are effective lattice-dominated thermal conductivities measured via TDTR (paper treats these as lattice thermal conductivities).
extracted_data.unstrained_or_reference_case: References to bulk Si1-xGex literature values and to Si/Ge superlattice measurements are used as reference controls; authors state measured film kappas are ~3–5× lower than bulk values (bulk values taken from literature), and compare to previously published thin-film and superlattice data plotted in Fig.2 and Fig.5.
extracted_data.observed_strain_effect_summary: The authors do not report or quantify strain-induced changes. Instead, they find that finite sample thickness (boundary scattering) dominates reductions in thermal conductivity of epitaxial Si1-xGex thin films; alloying has a reduced effect on k for thin films (0.2<x<0.8) compared to bulk. Dislocation density increases with thickness but does not explain the observed k trends.
extracted_data.phonon_dispersion_or_velocity_changes: No experimental or computed claims of strain-induced changes in phonon dispersion or group velocities are reported. The modeling assumes a dispersionless (Debye) system and uses a sound speed v in τ_b = d/v, but v is not reported as strain-dependent.
extracted_data.anharmonicity_metrics: Umklapp scattering is included via τ_U with phenomenological form τ_U^{-1} = B ω^2 exp(-C/T) (B and C taken from literature/Ref.[31]); no Grüneisen parameters, explicit anharmonic IFCs, or strain-dependent anharmonicity metrics are reported.
extracted_data.phonon_lifetimes_or_mfp: No mode-resolved lifetimes are tabulated. The paper uses relaxation-time expressions (τ_U, τ_α, τ_b) in the Debye RTA model. Spectral analysis (Fig.4) shows that dominant heat-carrying phonons are low-frequency (long-wavelength) modes; authors cite Garg et al. [21] who found that more than half of heat-carrying phonons in Si1-xGex can have mean free paths > 1 μm. The paper reports the spectral integrand peak frequencies ~10 rad s^-1 (for 427 nm) and ~10^3 rad s^-1 (for 39 nm) as qualitative indicators of frequency contributions (as plotted in Fig.4).
extracted_data.scattering_mechanisms_considered: Explicitly included in model: boundary scattering (τ_b = d/v), alloy (mass-disorder) scattering (τ_α = [x(1-x) A ω^4]^{-1}), and Umklapp scattering (τ_U with B, C parameters). Discussed but not dominant: dislocation scattering (defect densities measured by TEM, but authors conclude dislocations do not drive observed trends). Interface/superlattice scattering is discussed in comparisons (superlattice vs alloy thickness effects). Isotope, electron-phonon, or explicit strain-field scattering channels are not analyzed in this work.
extracted_data.interfaces_and_boundary_conditions: Films are on Si substrates with an Al transducer layer for TDTR; aluminum thickness measured but interface thermal boundary resistance (TBR) is not reported separately. Boundary scattering is treated via τ_b = d/v (diffuse limiting assumption implied); no specularity parameter p is reported or fitted. For superlattices discussed from literature, authors note total sample thickness influences k more than period, but do not extract interface resistances here.
extracted_data.theoretical_model_and_key_parameters: Debye (dispersionless) relaxation-time approximation (RTA) model (Eq.1). Key relations used: τ_total via Matthiessen of τ_U, τ_α, τ_b. τ_α = [x(1-x) A ω^4]^{-1} (alloy/tamura-like ω^4 dependence), τ_b = d/v, τ_U,Si^{-1} = B_Si ω^2 exp(-C_Si/T) and similarly for Ge; effective τ_U = [(1-x) τ_{U,Si}^{-1} + x τ_{U,Ge}^{-1}]^{-1}. Constants A, B, C taken from Ref.[31]. Cutoff frequency ω_c = 2π v / a where a is Vegard-law lattice constant. Model assumes dispersionless phonons and is intended for nondilute alloy compositions.
extracted_data.mode_resolved_or_spectral_results: Paper provides frequency-resolved spectral integrand (Fig.4): low-frequency modes dominate heat transport in films, with spectral peak shifting with thickness (peak around low frequencies for 427 nm and to higher frequencies for 39 nm), and inset shows boundary scattering time τ_b is the shortest (limiting) for modes carrying most heat; alloy scattering dominates at high frequencies. No explicit LA/TA/optical branch-resolved numeric breakdown is provided.
extracted_data.confounding_factors_and_limitations: Authors note increased dislocation density with thickness (possible partial relaxation) but show k does not scale with dislocation density as expected if dislocations dominated scattering. The model is a Debye, dispersionless RTA approximation (limitation for detailed dispersion effects). TDTR provides an effective through-thickness k and cannot separate in-plane vs cross-plane components. No quantitative strain state or strain magnitudes are provided; therefore direct strain–k relations cannot be assessed from this paper. Model parameters are taken from literature (Ref.[31]) and not extracted from first-principles for the samples. Uncertainty sources: film thickness, Al thickness, and measurement scatter (accounted in reported uncertainties).
extracted_data.key_figures_or_tables: Table I: lists film thicknesses, Ge content, and measured thermal conductivities; Fig.2: measured k vs period/film thickness and comparison to literature superlattice/alloy data; Fig.3: measured k vs Ge concentration and model predictions for bulk and thin-film thicknesses; Fig.4: spectral contribution (integrand) of modes to k and relative scattering times showing boundary scattering dominance at low frequencies; Fig.5: temperature dependence of k (141–300 K) for selected films and comparison to superlattice data and bulk/dilute/alloy curves.

theory-1.name: Tetragonal-phonon-transport renormalization under coherent biaxial strain (refined)
theory-1.description:
Coherent growth on a (001) Si/Ge substrate imposes an in-plane lattice constraint that converts an originally cubic (diamond-structure) material into a tetragonally distorted one. This symmetry reduction generically (i) creates direction-dependent acoustic velocities through strain-renormalized elastic constants and (ii) modifies intrinsic anharmonic scattering by shifting mode frequencies and their strain sensitivity (Grüneisen response), which changes three-phonon phase space and matrix elements. In alloys, strong mass-disorder scattering often dominates, so strain-induced changes in lifetimes are typically secondary and the net κ changes can be modest in magnitude but anisotropic in sign.

For the mission case (coherent Si0.5Ge0.5 on Si(001), ~2% in-plane compression), the theory predicts a weak-to-moderate anisotropy: in-plane κ tends to increase (in-plane stiffening/velocity increase), while cross-plane κ tends to decrease slightly or show little change because the out-of-plane response may soften and/or gain additional phase space for scattering in the tetragonal crystal, and because alloy scattering already strongly limits mean free paths at 300 K. At 300 K, the most likely cross-plane change relative to relaxed bulk Si0.5Ge0.5 is a small decrease on the order of ~5–12% (category: decrease).
theory-1.theory_query: Build theories of how biaxial strain (coherent growth on Si or Ge substrates) changes the in-plane and cross-plane lattice thermal conductivity of Si1-xGex films and of strained silicon and germanium, through changes in phonon group velocities, anharmonicity and scattering, based on the following results.

components.theory_name_plain_language: Coherent biaxial strain makes thermal conductivity direction-dependent by changing phonon speeds and scattering differently in-plane vs cross-plane
components.theory_description:

For the mission case (coherent Si0.5Ge0.5 on Si(001), ~2% in-plane compression), the theory predicts a weak-to-moderate anisotropy: in-plane κ tends to increase (in-plane stiffening/velocity increase), while cross-plane κ tends to decrease slightly or show little change because the out-of-plane response may soften and/or gain additional phase space for scattering in the tetragonal crystal, and because alloy scattering already strongly limits mean free paths at 300 K. components.theory_description_plain_language: Biaxial strain from coherent epitaxy turns a cubic crystal into a tetragonal one. That changes phonon speeds and phonon-phonon scattering differently along the plane and through the thickness, so in-plane and cross-plane thermal conductivities can change in different directions. In SiGe alloys the net effect is usually modest because alloy scattering is already strong.

law.statement_name: Coherent biaxial constraint implies tetragonal distortion and potential κ anisotropy
law.theory_statement: If a diamond-cubic Si/Ge/Si1-xGex film is coherently constrained on a (001) substrate such that the in-plane lattice parameter is fixed (biaxial epitaxial strain ε∥) while the out-of-plane parameter relaxes elastically (ε⊥ determined by elastic compatibility), then the crystal symmetry is reduced from cubic to tetragonal. This symmetry reduction generically permits direction-dependent phonon dispersions and sound speeds (v∥ ≠ v⊥) and therefore permits (and typically induces) anisotropic lattice thermal conductivity components κ∥ and κ⊥, even when the unstrained bulk is isotropic.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: Coherent biaxial strain makes the lattice tetragonal, so phonon speeds (and thus thermal conductivity) can differ in-plane and cross-plane.
law.domain_scope: Coherently strained (pseudomorphic) Si, Ge, and Si1-xGex films on (001) Si/Ge or virtual substrates, in regimes where heat transport is dominated by lattice phonons (i.e., not dominated by electronic κ at extreme doping) and where the film can be treated as a homogeneous tetragonal elastic medium (ignoring patterned nanostructures).
special_cases: If the film partially/fully relaxes via misfit dislocations, the average tetragonal distortion (and any intrinsic κ anisotropy from coherence) is reduced; extrinsic dislocation scattering may dominate instead.
In ultrathin freestanding membranes with reconstructed surfaces, surface states/reconstructions can dominate strain response of κ, and substrate-coherent epitaxy arguments may not transfer directly.
For extremely small strains, induced anisotropy may be below experimental/MD noise floors even if symmetry arguments allow it.

supporting_evidence.text: Epitaxial Ge on Si(001) is described as biaxially strained with tetragonal distortion confirmed by high-resolution XRD reciprocal-space maps; the analysis explicitly treats anisotropic (parallel vs perpendicular) thermal expansion under epitaxial constraint.

Ge1-xSnx layers grown on Ge/Si are likewise treated as tetragonally distorted biaxial epilayers under substrate/buffer constraint; Raman and XRD strains are compared and modeled with an anisotropic epitaxial-constraint framework.

A computational study applies biaxial in-plane strain to Si thin films and finds strain-tunable in-plane κ with mode-resolved changes in phonon properties, consistent with strain-induced alteration of phonon transport properties under biaxial constraint (though in a freestanding geometry).

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: It is well known that coherent biaxial strain reduces cubic symmetry to tetragonal and can make elastic/phonon properties anisotropic; phonon-transport anisotropy under broken symmetry is a standard expectation.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: This law frames κ anisotropy as the default symmetry-permitted outcome of coherent epitaxy (rather than an interface/defect artifact) and explicitly scopes it to SiGe alloys where intrinsic changes compete with strong alloy scattering.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: The symmetry argument itself is established, but its explicit use as a predictive organizing principle for κ∥ vs κ⊥ in coherently strained Si1-xGex (including mid-alloy compositions) is a synthesis beyond the provided sources.
references: Li (2010) Strain effects on the thermal conductivity of nanostructures [review/theory linking strain to κ changes via phonons]
Parrish (year not provided) [as cited] isotropic tensile strain reduces κ in bulk Si [existing computational observation of strain–κ coupling]
Ziman (1960) Electrons and Phonons [foundational kinetic picture underlying anisotropic transport when v and τ are anisotropic]

law.statement_name: Directional κ change under biaxial strain is governed by velocity renormalization versus scattering renormalization
law.theory_statement: For small-to-moderate coherent biaxial strain in Si/Ge/SiGe at temperatures where phonon transport is well described by a phonon gas with dominant three-phonon processes (typically near and above room temperature), the directional lattice conductivity may be approximated as κi ≈ Σm C_m v_{m,i}^2 τ_m (i ∈ {∥, ⊥}). Therefore the fractional directional change obeys Δκi/κi ≈ ⟨2Δv_{m,i}/v_{m,i} + Δτ_m/τ_m⟩_weighted + (small ΔC/C). Under biaxial strain, Δv_{m,∥} and Δv_{m,⊥} can have opposite signs (tetragonal elastic response), while Δτ_m/τ_m is controlled by strain-altered anharmonicity and three-phonon phase space (often expressible through Grüneisen-like frequency–strain sensitivities). Net sign and anisotropy follow from which contribution dominates in each direction; in strongly alloy-scattering-limited SiGe (e.g., near x≈0.5) |Δτ| from intrinsic anharmonicity is often a subleading correction, so |Δκ| is modest even at percent-level strain.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: Strain changes thermal conductivity by changing phonon speeds and phonon lifetimes; direction-by-direction, whichever changes more determines whether κ goes up or down, and alloy scattering often makes the total change small.
law.domain_scope: Crystalline Si, Ge, and random-alloy Si1-xGex in the temperature range where phonon heat capacity is near classical and intrinsic phonon-phonon scattering matters (roughly 200–600 K), excluding regimes dominated by electronic κ or glass-like transport; applies to coherent biaxial strain states (tetragonal distortion) and to unpatterned films where bulk-like phonons remain meaningful carriers.
special_cases: In ultrathin freestanding films, strain-induced surface reconstruction/topological-surface-mode changes can dominate κ trends, breaking a simple bulk-like velocity/stiffness intuition.
When boundary scattering dominates (very thin films or very rough interfaces), τ is capped by τ_b ≈ d/v and intrinsic strain-induced τ changes have limited impact.
When strong extrinsic scattering exists (high dislocation density, precipitates), κ changes may be dominated by defect scattering rather than intrinsic anharmonicity renormalization.

supporting_evidence.text: The strained-Ge epilayer analysis extracts anisotropic Grüneisen parameters (γ∥, γ⊥) and an explicit anharmonic coefficient A3, indicating that epitaxial strain changes phonon frequency–strain response and explicit anharmonic renormalization parameters that would affect three-phonon scattering and thus τ.

For Ge/Si, A3 is larger in the epitaxial strained layer than in bulk Ge (A3 bulk ≈ 0.77 cm−1; A3 epilayer ≈ 1.0 cm−1), consistent with potentially stronger intrinsic anharmonic effects (shorter τ) in strained material, all else equal.

For GeSn epilayers, fitted γ values are similar (≈1.3) and A3 shows little dependence on composition and threading dislocation density, supporting the notion that changes in κ across similar alloys are more governed by disorder scattering than by large changes in intrinsic anharmonicity parameters.

The electronic-transport paper cites prior computational literature that tensile strain reduces κ in bulk Si (e.g., ~10% reduction at 3% isotropic tensile strain) and attributes reductions to reduced phonon group velocities and/or specific heat—consistent with the velocity/lifetime decomposition framework.

The biaxially strained Si thin-film computational study explicitly computes mode-resolved group velocities and lifetimes and shows κ is strain-tunable, directly supporting the principle that κ changes can be decomposed into v and τ changes under biaxial strain (though for freestanding thin films).

Cheaito et al. show that in SiGe thin films, boundary scattering can dominate low-frequency heat-carrying phonons (size effects) and alloy scattering dominates high frequencies; this supports the special case that when extrinsic/boundary/alloy scattering caps τ, additional intrinsic strain-induced τ changes will have muted impact on κ magnitude.

This law/statement was logically inferred by combining the standard kinetic form κ ~ Σ C v^2 τ with evidence that (i) strain modifies phonon parameters linked to anharmonicity (γ, A3) and (ii) literature attributes strain effects to group-velocity/specific-heat changes; the directional form under biaxial strain is an anisotropic extension of these elements.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: The kinetic-theory structure κ ~ C v^2 τ and the idea that strain changes v and τ are well established; Grüneisen parameters are widely used to relate strain to frequency shifts and anharmonic trends.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: The statement makes an explicit, direction-resolved competition rule for coherent biaxial (tetragonal) strain and emphasizes that in mid-alloy SiGe the strain effect is typically modest because τ is already limited by alloy/boundary scattering—yielding a practical predictive hierarchy for κ∥ vs κ⊥.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: Grounded in existing transport theory, but the explicit anisotropic, coherent-epitaxy framing plus the dominance-ordering (alloy/boundary first, strain-renormalized intrinsic scattering second) is a synthesis not directly stated in any one provided source.
references: Ziman (1960) Electrons and Phonons [κ ~ C v^2 τ framework]
Broido (2007) Intrinsic lattice thermal conductivity of semiconductors from first principles [role of three-phonon scattering and anharmonicity in τ]
Cheaito (2012) Experimental Investigation of Size Effects on the Thermal Conductivity of Silicon-Germanium Alloy Thin Films [evidence for boundary/alloy limiting τ in SiGe thin films]

new_predictions_likely: For coherently compressed Si0.5Ge0.5 on Si(001) at 300 K, κ⊥ (cross-plane) will fall slightly relative to relaxed bulk (category: decrease), with a likely magnitude of ~5–12% decrease, while κ∥ increases modestly (few to ~10%) due to in-plane stiffening.

For coherently strained Ge on Si(001), if one could isolate an otherwise defect-free epilayer, an increased A3 relative to bulk would correlate with reduced intrinsic τ and thus reduced κ compared with unstrained bulk at the same T, despite any stiffness-related v increases.

In SiGe films where thickness/boundary scattering is already the shortest scattering time (as in Cheaito’s thin films), imposing additional coherent biaxial strain will change κ less (smaller |Δκ|) than in thicker, bulk-like samples at the same composition.
new_predictions_unknown: A sign change with temperature for κ⊥ under coherent compression near x≈0.5: κ⊥ may decrease at 300 K but show weaker decrease or even slight increase at cryogenic temperatures if intrinsic three-phonon scattering becomes weak and velocity anisotropy dominates over strain-modified anharmonicity.

At sufficiently large coherent biaxial strain (few percent) in SiGe, tetragonal splitting could nonlinearly increase three-phonon phase space for particular cross-plane polarized modes, producing a larger κ anisotropy than predicted by linear-elastic velocity changes alone.
negative_experiments: Perform spectral (mode-resolved) analysis for coherently strained Si0.5Ge0.5 and test whether strain changes (i) v∥ vs v⊥ and/or (ii) τ in a directionally correlated way; if neither v nor τ show meaningful anisotropy but κ does, the mechanism assignment is incomplete.

Compare a coherently strained film to a plastically relaxed film of the same composition and thickness: if both show the same κ anisotropy, then coherence-induced tetragonal distortion is not the dominant cause (microstructure/interface effects would be implicated).

In an alloy composition where τ is known to be alloy-scattering-limited, measure Δκ under strain; if Δκ is as large as in pure Si/Ge under comparable strain, then the 'alloy-scattering mutes strain response' component is falsified.

unaccounted_for.text: Direct measurements or simulations of κ∥ and κ⊥ in coherently strained Si1-xGex (especially x=0.5) are not present in the provided evidence; therefore, magnitude calibration for the predicted percent changes remains uncertain.

conflicting_evidence.text: The strained-Si thin-film computational work attributes much of the strain sensitivity of κ to strain-modulated surface reconstructions and topological surface phonons in freestanding ultrathin membranes; this may not apply to substrate-supported epitaxial SiGe films where free-surface reconstructions and topological surface modes are different or suppressed.

special_cases: Ultrathin freestanding films/membranes: surface reconstructions and surface/topological phonons can dominate κ and its strain dependence (nonmonotonic trends possible).
Partially relaxed epitaxial films: misfit dislocations reduce coherent tetragonal distortion and add strong extrinsic scattering that can overwhelm intrinsic strain renormalization.
Very thin substrate-supported films where boundary scattering dominates: intrinsic strain-induced changes to τ have limited leverage on κ.

references: Li (2010) Strain effects on the thermal conductivity of nanostructures [strain–κ coupling via modified phonon properties]
Parrish (year not provided) [as cited] isotropic tensile strain reduces κ in bulk Si [existing computational observation]
Cheaito (2012) Experimental Investigation of Size Effects on the Thermal Conductivity of Silicon-Germanium Alloy Thin Films [size/alloy scattering hierarchy in SiGe films]
existing_theory.what_already_exists: Strain can change κ by modifying phonon dispersions (v) and anharmonic scattering (τ); alloy and boundary scattering often dominate κ reductions in SiGe thin films.
existing_theory.what_is_novel: A coherent-epitaxy-centered, direction-resolved hierarchy for predicting κ∥ vs κ⊥ changes in SiGe under biaxial strain, with an explicit sign forecast for coherent compression near x=0.5.
existing_theory.classification_explanation: Uses standard phonon transport theory but adds a specific coherent-biaxial/tetragonal and alloy-limited predictive structure not explicitly provided by the cited evidence set.

theory-2.name: Alloy-dominated scattering with strain-as-perturbation in Si1-xGex films
theory-2.description: In Si1-xGex films, especially near mid-composition, mass-disorder (alloy) scattering with a strong ω^4-like scaling and boundary/thickness scattering frequently set the dominant phonon lifetimes and thus the baseline κ. Coherent biaxial strain then acts mainly as a perturbation that slightly renormalizes group velocities and intrinsic Umklapp rates, producing comparatively small fractional κ changes at 300 K relative to the large absolute suppression already caused by alloying and finite thickness. The perturbation can still be anisotropic (different in-plane vs cross-plane response), but the magnitude is constrained by Matthiessen’s rule: if τ_alloy and τ_boundary are already short, changing τ_U or v by a few percent cannot move κ by tens of percent.
theory-2.theory_query: Build theories of how biaxial strain (coherent growth on Si or Ge substrates) changes the in-plane and cross-plane lattice thermal conductivity of Si1-xGex films and of strained silicon and germanium, through changes in phonon group velocities, anharmonicity and scattering, based on the following results.

components.theory_name: Alloy-dominated scattering with strain-as-perturbation in Si1-xGex films
components.theory_name_plain_language: In SiGe alloys, strain tweaks phonons but alloy/boundary scattering sets the baseline
components.theory_description: In Si1-xGex films, especially near mid-composition, mass-disorder (alloy) scattering with a strong ω^4-like scaling and boundary/thickness scattering frequently set the dominant phonon lifetimes and thus the baseline κ. Coherent biaxial strain then acts mainly as a perturbation that slightly renormalizes group velocities and intrinsic Umklapp rates, producing comparatively small fractional κ changes at 300 K relative to the large absolute suppression already caused by alloying and finite thickness. The perturbation can still be anisotropic (different in-plane vs cross-plane response), but the magnitude is constrained by Matthiessen’s rule: if τ_alloy and τ_boundary are already short, changing τ_U or v by a few percent cannot move κ by tens of percent.
components.theory_description_plain_language: SiGe films already have low thermal conductivity because alloy disorder and film thickness strongly scatter phonons. Strain can still change κ, but usually only by a small amount because the lifetimes are already limited by those stronger scattering mechanisms.

law.statement_name: Matthiessen-limited strain leverage on κ in alloy/thin-film regime
law.theory_statement: In Si1-xGex films where total scattering satisfies τ_total^{-1} = τ_U^{-1} + τ_alloy^{-1} + τ_b^{-1} and τ_alloy^{-1} and/or τ_b^{-1} dominate over τ_U^{-1} for heat-carrying modes, coherent biaxial strain-induced changes to intrinsic anharmonic scattering (τ_U) and modest changes to v produce only limited fractional changes in κ (typically single-digit to low-teens percent at room temperature), because τ_total is capped by the shortest channels.
law.theory_statement_plain_language: When alloy and boundary scattering already dominate, strain can only change thermal conductivity a little because lifetimes are already short.
law.domain_scope: Epitaxial or crystalline Si1-xGex films (tens of nm to sub-micron and thicker) in which alloy disorder and/or boundary scattering are significant; most applicable near room temperature where Umklapp exists but is not necessarily dominant in alloys; applies regardless of whether the film is fully coherent, provided alloy/boundary scattering dominate phonon lifetimes.
special_cases: In very pure Si or Ge (x near 0 or 1) and thick samples where τ_U dominates, strain can produce larger fractional κ changes.

If strain introduces/disables additional extrinsic scattering sources (e.g., misfit dislocations upon partial relaxation), κ can change strongly, but that is not an intrinsic coherent-strain perturbation.

supporting_evidence.text: Cheaito et al. model Si1-xGex thin films with Matthiessen’s rule combining Umklapp, alloy scattering τ_α = [x(1-x)A ω^4]^{-1}, and boundary scattering τ_b = d/v, and conclude boundary scattering of long-wavelength phonons dominates κ reductions in thin films; alloy scattering dominates at high frequencies.

Cheaito et al. measure very low cross-plane κ in SiGe thin films (e.g., ~1.8–2.8 W/m-K for Si0.8Ge0.2 across 39–427 nm), illustrating that κ is already strongly suppressed by alloying/size compared with bulk, implying limited headroom for additional modest strain effects.

Raman/XRD analysis of GeSn indicates A3 and γ show little dependence on composition or threading dislocation density in the studied range, supporting the idea that disorder/alloy scattering dominates κ variations rather than large strain-induced changes to intrinsic anharmonicity parameters.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Use of Matthiessen’s rule and the dominance of alloy/boundary scattering in SiGe thin films are established modeling ideas.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: This law explicitly constrains the magnitude of coherent-strain-induced κ changes in mid-alloy SiGe films by combining (i) the dominance hierarchy seen in thin-film SiGe with (ii) the fact that strain mostly perturbs intrinsic channels.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: Mechanistically consistent with existing models, but the explicit 'limited strain leverage' quantitative expectation for room-temperature SiGe films is a synthesized predictive guideline.
references: Cheaito (2012) Experimental Investigation of Size Effects on the Thermal Conductivity of Silicon-Germanium Alloy Thin Films [Matthiessen + dominance of boundary scattering]
Tamura (1983) Isotope scattering of dispersive phonons in Ge [basis for ω^4-like mass-disorder scattering used widely for alloys]

law.statement_name: Thickness control can mask strain dependence in cross-plane κ measurements
law.theory_statement: For cross-plane thermal conductivity measurements of SiGe films on substrates (e.g., TDTR-style effective through-thickness κ), if boundary/thickness scattering limits the mean free paths of the dominant low-frequency heat-carrying phonons, then the observed κ⊥ will be primarily controlled by film thickness d (through τ_b ≈ d/v) and only weakly sensitive to coherent biaxial strain unless strain strongly modifies v⊥ or introduces additional extrinsic scattering (e.g., dislocations).
law.theory_statement_plain_language: If thickness is the main limiter of cross-plane heat flow, strain won’t change the measured cross-plane κ very much.
law.domain_scope: Substrate-supported Si1-xGex thin films where through-thickness κ is extracted as an effective value and where size effects are significant (tens to hundreds of nm, potentially up to sub-micron depending on MFP spectrum); room temperature and below where long-MFP phonons would otherwise contribute strongly.
special_cases: At very large thickness (approaching bulk) or very smooth/specular boundaries, size limitation weakens and intrinsic strain effects can become more visible.
If the strain state changes with thickness due to relaxation, thickness trends can entangle strain and defect effects.

supporting_evidence.text: Cheaito et al. conclude boundary scattering of long-wavelength phonons dominates κ reductions in epitaxial SiGe thin films; their spectral analysis indicates τ_b is the shortest (limiting) for modes carrying most heat in the thinnest films.

Cheaito et al. compare thin-film alloys and superlattices and argue total sample thickness controls κ similarly, consistent with size-limited scattering of long-wavelength phonons dominating over other mechanisms in many thin samples.

novelty_evaluation.what_already_exists: Size effects and boundary-limited κ in thin films are well known, and Cheaito explicitly emphasizes them for SiGe.
novelty_evaluation.what_is_novel: This law makes an explicit measurement-level prediction: cross-plane κ trends in strained/coherent films can appear strain-insensitive simply because thickness-limited transport masks intrinsic strain renormalization.
novelty_evaluation.classification_explanation: Directly motivated by the provided thin-film evidence but framed as a general caution/predictive rule for interpreting strain effects in cross-plane κ experiments/simulations.
references: Cheaito (2012) Experimental Investigation of Size Effects on the Thermal Conductivity of Silicon-Germanium Alloy Thin Films [size dominance in κ]
Balandin (1998) phonon confinement in semiconductor quantum wells [classic size-effect framing in thin films]

new_predictions_likely: For Si0.5Ge0.5 films where alloy scattering dominates, coherent biaxial strain of ~2% will change κ by at most low-teens percent at 300 K, even if anisotropic (κ∥ and κ⊥ can shift in opposite directions).

If two SiGe films have the same thickness and composition but different coherent strain states (within the elastic stability range) and remain dislocation-free, κ differences will be smaller than differences caused by changing thickness by a factor of ~2 in the size-limited regime.
In TDTR-style cross-plane measurements, the strain dependence of extracted κ⊥ will be weakest in the thinnest films (tens of nm), where τ_b dominates.
new_predictions_unknown: In mid-alloy SiGe, sufficiently large coherent strain might shift the dominant heat-carrying spectrum toward frequencies where alloy scattering is weaker/stronger, producing a non-intuitive strain dependence (including potential nonmonotonic κ vs strain).

If coherent strain significantly changes the acoustic–optical gap in SiGe alloys, it could alter the relative importance of Umklapp channels and amplify strain effects beyond the Matthiessen-limited expectation.
negative_experiments: If a mid-alloy SiGe film (x≈0.5) with strong alloy scattering exhibits a >30% κ change under modest coherent strain without introducing dislocations, this theory’s 'limited leverage' claim is falsified.

If thinning a SiGe film does not reduce κ in the manner predicted by τ_b ≈ d/v dominance (holding composition constant), then the assumed dominance of boundary scattering for long-wavelength phonons is incorrect for that system.

If mode-resolved analysis shows τ_U dominates over τ_alloy for the heat-carrying spectrum at x≈0.5 and 300 K, then intrinsic strain-induced changes to τ_U could be large and this theory’s hierarchy would not apply.

unaccounted_for.text: The provided evidence does not include any direct strained/coherent Si0.5Ge0.5 κ data (in-plane or cross-plane) to numerically validate the magnitude bounds suggested here.

special_cases: Pure Si/Ge limits (x→0 or 1): alloy scattering weakens and strain effects on intrinsic κ can become comparatively larger.
Strain relaxation with dislocations: can strongly reduce κ via defect scattering, overwhelming the intrinsic perturbative picture.

references: Cheaito (2012) Experimental Investigation of Size Effects on the Thermal Conductivity of Silicon-Germanium Alloy Thin Films [dominance of boundary/alloy scattering in thin films]
Callaway (1959) Model for lattice thermal conductivity at low temperatures [Matthiessen-style combination of scattering processes]

existing_theory.what_is_novel: A strain-focused corollary: coherent biaxial strain is expected to have limited impact on κ magnitude in mid-alloy, size-limited films because it perturbs subdominant channels.
existing_theory.classification_explanation: Mostly an application/extension of established scattering-hierarchy thinking to the specific question of coherent-strain tuning in SiGe.

theory-3.name: Alloy-dominance attenuation: strain as a second-order perturbation in Si0.5Ge0.5 (corrected)
theory-3.description:
In concentrated random-substitutional Si1-xGex alloys near x≈0.5, mass-disorder (alloy) scattering suppresses phonon lifetimes strongly over a broad spectrum. Coherent biaxial strain (tetragonal distortion from pseudomorphic growth on Si or Ge) primarily perturbs harmonic properties (elastic constants, mode splitting, sound speeds) and intrinsic anharmonicity (three-phonon scattering strength). At room temperature, these strain-induced perturbations usually act as smaller corrections to already-short lifetimes set by alloy disorder and (in thin films) boundary scattering. Therefore, provided the film remains coherent and does not introduce additional extrinsic scattering (misfit dislocations, high TDD, roughness changes), the net strain-induced change in lattice thermal conductivity is expected to be modest (single-digit to low-teens percent) but anisotropic because the tetragonal symmetry breaking modifies in-plane and cross-plane dispersions differently.

Applied to the mission case H7 (Si0.5Ge0.5 coherently grown on Si(001), ~2% in-plane compression): the theory predicts cross-plane κ at 300 K is most likely to DECREASE slightly (category: decrease; best estimate about −5% to −12%, nominal point estimate −8%) relative to relaxed bulk Si0.5Ge0.5. In-plane κ is expected to be unchanged to slightly increased (0% to +8%, nominal +3% to +5%) because in-plane elastic stiffening tends to raise in-plane acoustic group velocities while alloy scattering keeps lifetime changes small. These magnitude ranges are intended for intrinsic lattice κ (as computed in bulk-like MD/BTE) rather than TDTR effective κ that can be dominated by interface thermal boundary resistance.

components.theory_name: Alloy-dominance attenuation: strain as a second-order perturbation in Si0.5Ge0.5 (corrected)
components.theory_name_plain_language: At 50/50 SiGe, alloy disorder dominates; coherent strain only tweaks thermal conductivity (anisotropically)
