metadata.title: Effect of strain on the thermoelectric properties of silicon: an ab initio study

tldr.text: The anisotropic thermoelectric transport properties of biaxially strained silicon were studied with the focus on a possible enhancement of the power factor to understand the fact that the thermopower decreases if degenerate bands are energetically lifted due to a strain-induced redistribution of states.

metadata.abstract: On the basis of detailed first-principles calculations the anisotropic thermoelectric transport properties of biaxially strained silicon were studied with the focus on a possible enhancement of the power factor. Electron as well as hole doping was examined in a broad doping and temperature range. In the low temperature and low doping regime an enhancement of the power factor was obtained for compressive and tensile strain in the electron-doped case, and for compressive strain in the hole-doped case. In the thermoelectrically more important high temperature and high doping regime a slight enhancement of the power factor was only found for the hole-doped case under small biaxial tensile strain. The results are discussed in terms of band structure effects. An analytical model is presented to understand the fact that the thermopower decreases if degenerate bands are energetically lifted due to a strain-induced redistribution of states.

metadata.title: Experimental investigation of size effects on the thermal conductivity of silicon-germanium alloy thin films.

tldr.text: It is found that the thermal conductivities of Si(1-x)Ge(x) superlattices are ultimately limited by finite size effects and sample size rather than periodicity or alloying, demonstrating the strong influence of sample size in alloyed nanosystems.

metadata.abstract: We experimentally investigate the role of size effects and boundary scattering on the thermal conductivity of silicon-germanium alloys. The thermal conductivities of a series of epitaxially grown Si(1-x)Ge(x) thin films with varying thicknesses and compositions were measured with time-domain thermoreflectance. The resulting conductivities are found to be 3 to 5 times less than bulk values and vary strongly with film thickness. By examining these measured thermal conductivities in the context of a previously established model, it is shown that long wavelength phonons, known to be the dominant heat carriers in alloy films, are strongly scattered by the film boundaries, thereby inducing the observed reductions in heat transport. These results are then generalized to silicon-germanium systems of various thicknesses and compositions; we find that the thermal conductivities of Si(1-x)Ge(x) superlattices are ultimately limited by finite size effects and sample size rather than periodicity or alloying. This demonstrates the strong influence of sample size in alloyed nanosystems. Therefore, if a comparison is to be made between the thermal conductivities of superlattices and alloys, the total sample thicknesses of each must be considered.

| growth_and_microstructure | Epitaxial growth by metal-organic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD); film stoichiometry by Rutherford backscattering, thickness by x-ray reflectivity and cross-sectional TEM, surface roughness by AFM. Plan-view TEM shows dislocation density increases with film thickness; defects present especially in thicker films. No quantitative interface roughness or coherent-layer claim is given. |

Films are epitaxial on Si(001) and thus may experience biaxial lattice mismatch strain for some thicknesses/compositions, but TEM shows increasing dislocation density with thickness indicating partial relaxation/relaxed state for thicker films; authors do not claim fully coherent pseudomorphic films. |
| strain_magnitude | Not reported; no quantitative in-plane or out-of-plane strain values, mismatch percentages, or c/a distortions provided. |
| film_thickness_and_geometry | Measured film thicknesses (thickness series, Si0.8Ge0.2): 39 ± 0.9 nm, 88 ± 1.8 nm, 202 ± 2.1 nm, 427 ± 2.1 nm. Composition series: 88 ± 1.8 nm (20.0% Ge), 135 ± 10.4 nm (34.5% Ge), 126 ± 10.1 nm (45.0% Ge). Films coated with an Al transducer for TDTR. |

| measurement_or_simulation_method | Experimental: Time-domain thermoreflectance (TDTR), double-color pump-probe with Al transducer; Al thickness confirmed by picosecond acoustics. Modeling/analysis: analytic Debye, dispersionless relaxation-time approximation (RTA) model (Eq. (1) in paper) with Matthiessen's rule combining Umklapp (τ_U), alloy (τ_α), and boundary (τ_b) scattering. Model constants A, B, C taken from Ref. [31]; cutoff frequency ω_c = 2π v / a with lattice constant a from Vegard's law. |
| reported_kappa_in_plane | Not reported (no separate in-plane thermal conductivity measurements provided). |
| reported_kappa_cross_plane | Reported effective through-thickness thermal conductivity (W m^-1 K^-1) measured by TDTR: For 20.0% Ge thickness series: 39 nm: 1.83 ± 0.09 W m^-1 K^-1; 88 nm: 2.17 ± 0.10 W m^-1 K^-1; 202 nm: 2.69 ± 0.10 W m^-1 K^-1; 427 nm: 2.84 ± 0.18 W m^-1 K^-1. Composition-series: 88 nm (20.0% Ge): 2.17 ± 0.10 W m^-1 K^-1; 135 nm (34.5% Ge): 1.68 ± 0.30 W m^-1 K^-1; 126 nm (45.0% Ge): 1.79 ± 0.39 W m^-1 K^-1. Values are effective lattice-dominated thermal conductivities measured via TDTR (paper treats these as lattice thermal conductivities). |
| kappa_anisotropy_metric | None |
| unstrained_or_reference_case | References to bulk Si1-xGex literature values and to Si/Ge superlattice measurements are used as reference controls; authors state measured film kappas are ~3–5× lower than bulk values (bulk values taken from literature), and compare to previously published thin-film and superlattice data plotted in Fig.2 and Fig.5. |
| observed_strain_effect_summary | The authors do not report or quantify strain-induced changes. Instead, they find that finite sample thickness (boundary scattering) dominates reductions in thermal conductivity of epitaxial Si1-xGex thin films; alloying has a reduced effect on k for thin films (0.2<x<0.8) compared to bulk. Dislocation density increases with thickness but does not explain the observed k trends. |
| phonon_dispersion_or_velocity_changes | No experimental or computed claims of strain-induced changes in phonon dispersion or group velocities are reported. The modeling assumes a dispersionless (Debye) system and uses a sound speed v in τ_b = d/v, but v is not reported as strain-dependent. |
| anharmonicity_metrics | Umklapp scattering is included via τ_U with phenomenological form τ_U^{-1} = B ω^2 exp(-C/T) (B and C taken from literature/Ref.[31]); no Grüneisen parameters, explicit anharmonic IFCs, or strain-dependent anharmonicity metrics are reported. |
| phonon_lifetimes_or_mfp | No mode-resolved lifetimes are tabulated. The paper uses relaxation-time expressions (τ_U, τ_α, τ_b) in the Debye RTA model. Spectral analysis (Fig.4) shows that dominant heat-carrying phonons are low-frequency (long-wavelength) modes; authors cite Garg et al. [21] who found that more than half of heat-carrying phonons in Si1-xGex can have mean free paths > 1 μm. The paper reports the spectral integrand peak frequencies ~10 rad s^-1 (for 427 nm) and ~10^3 rad s^-1 (for 39 nm) as qualitative indicators of frequency contributions (as plotted in Fig.4). |
| scattering_mechanisms_considered | Explicitly included in model: boundary scattering (τ_b = d/v), alloy (mass-disorder) scattering (τ_α = [x(1-x) A ω^4]^{-1}), and Umklapp scattering (τ_U with B, C parameters). Discussed but not dominant: dislocation scattering (defect densities measured by TEM, but authors conclude dislocations do not drive observed trends). Interface/superlattice scattering is discussed in comparisons (superlattice vs alloy thickness effects). Isotope, electron-phonon, or explicit strain-field scattering channels are not analyzed in this work. |
| interfaces_and_boundary_conditions | Films are on Si substrates with an Al transducer layer for TDTR; aluminum thickness measured but interface thermal boundary resistance (TBR) is not reported separately. Boundary scattering is treated via τ_b = d/v (diffuse limiting assumption implied); no specularity parameter p is reported or fitted. For superlattices discussed from literature, authors note total sample thickness influences k more than period, but do not extract interface resistances here. |
| theoretical_model_and_key_parameters | Debye (dispersionless) relaxation-time approximation (RTA) model (Eq.1). Key relations used: τ_total via Matthiessen of τ_U, τ_α, τ_b. τ_α = [x(1-x) A ω^4]^{-1} (alloy/tamura-like ω^4 dependence), τ_b = d/v, τ_U,Si^{-1} = B_Si ω^2 exp(-C_Si/T) and similarly for Ge; effective τ_U = [(1-x) τ_{U,Si}^{-1} + x τ_{U,Ge}^{-1}]^{-1}. Constants A, B, C taken from Ref.[31]. Cutoff frequency ω_c = 2π v / a where a is Vegard-law lattice constant. Model assumes dispersionless phonons and is intended for nondilute alloy compositions. |
| mode_resolved_or_spectral_results | Paper provides frequency-resolved spectral integrand (Fig.4): low-frequency modes dominate heat transport in films, with spectral peak shifting with thickness (peak around low frequencies for 427 nm and to higher frequencies for 39 nm), and inset shows boundary scattering time τ_b is the shortest (limiting) for modes carrying most heat; alloy scattering dominates at high frequencies. No explicit LA/TA/optical branch-resolved numeric breakdown is provided. |
| confounding_factors_and_limitations | Authors note increased dislocation density with thickness (possible partial relaxation) but show k does not scale with dislocation density as expected if dislocations dominated scattering. The model is a Debye, dispersionless RTA approximation (limitation for detailed dispersion effects). TDTR provides an effective through-thickness k and cannot separate in-plane vs cross-plane components. No quantitative strain state or strain magnitudes are provided; therefore direct strain–k relations cannot be assessed from this paper. Model parameters are taken from literature (Ref.[31]) and not extracted from first-principles for the samples. Uncertainty sources: film thickness, Al thickness, and measurement scatter (accounted in reported uncertainties). |
| key_figures_or_tables | Table I: lists film thicknesses, Ge content, and measured thermal conductivities; Fig.2: measured k vs period/film thickness and comparison to literature superlattice/alloy data; Fig.3: measured k vs Ge concentration and model predictions for bulk and thin-film thicknesses; Fig.4: spectral contribution (integrand) of modes to k and relative scattering times showing boundary scattering dominance at low frequencies; Fig.5: temperature dependence of k (141–300 K) for selected films and comparison to superlattice data and bulk/dilute/alloy curves. |

artifacts.description: Biaxial strain from coherent epitaxy turns a cubic crystal into a tetragonal one. That changes phonon speeds and phonon-phonon scattering differently along the plane and through the thickness, so in-plane and cross-plane thermal conductivities can change in different directions. In SiGe alloys the net effect is usually modest because alloy scattering is already strong.

<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>Ge</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mtext>−</mml:mtext><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mi>Sn<
s2Metadata.abstract: Temperature dependence of vibrational modes in semiconductors depends on lattice thermal expansion and anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering. Evaluating the two contributions from experimental data is not straightforward, especially for epitaxial layers that present mechanical deformation and anisotropic lattice expansion. In this work, a temperature-dependent Raman study in epitaxial Ge and Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$ layers is presented. A model is introduced for the Raman mode energy shift as a function of temperature, comprising thermal expansion of the strained lattice and anharmonic corrections. With support of x-ray diffraction, the model is calibrated on experimental data of epitaxial Ge grown on Si and Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$ grown on Ge/Si, finding that the main difference between bulk and epitaxial layers is related to the anisotropic lattice expansion. The phonon anharmonicity and other parameters do not depend on dislocation defect density (in the range $7\cdot 10^6$ - $4\cdot 10^8$ cm$^{-2}$) nor on alloy composition in the range 5-14 at.%. The strain-shift coefficient for the main model of Ge and for the Ge-Ge vibrational mode of Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$ is weakly dependent on temperature and is around -500 cm$^{-1}$. In Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$, the composition-shift coefficient amounts to -100 cm$^{-1}$, independent of temperature and strain.

paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c.displayLabel: Topological surface phonons modulate thermal transport in semiconductor thin films

s2Metadata.title: Topological surface phonons modulate thermal transport in semiconductor thin films
s2Metadata.abstract: While phonon topology in crystalline solids has been extensively studied, its influence on thermal transport-especially in nanostructures-remains elusive. Here, by combining first-principles-based machine learning potentials with the phonon Boltzmann transport equation and molecular dynamics simulations, we systematically investigate the role of topological surface phonons in the in-plane thermal transport of semiconductor thin films (Si, 4H -SiC, and c-BN). These topological surface phonons, originating from nontrivial acoustic phonon nodal lines, not only serve as key scattering channels for dominant acoustic phonons but also contribute substantially to the overall thermal conductivity. Remarkably, for these thin semiconductor films below 10 nm this contribution can be as large as over 30% of the in-plane thermal conductivity at 300 K, and the largest absolute contribution can reach 82 W/m-K, highlighting their significant role in nanoscale thermal transport in semiconductors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both temperature and biaxial strain provide effective means to modulate this contribution. Our work establishes a direct link between topological surface phonons and nanoscale thermal transport, offering the first quantitative assessment of their role and paving the way for topology-enabled thermal management in semiconductors.

paper-db50837f193e0e576acfdb1d75407a47f9.displayLabel: Reduced thermal conductivity of epitaxial GaAs on Si due to symmetry-breaking biaxial strain

s2Metadata.title: Reduced thermal conductivity of epitaxial GaAs on Si due to symmetry-breaking biaxial strain
s2Metadata.abstract: Epitaxial growth of III-V semiconductors on Si is a promising route for silicon photonics. Threading dislocations and the residual thermal stress generated during growth are expected to affect the thermal conductivity of the III-V semiconductors, which is crucial for efficient heat dissipation from photonic devices built on this platform. In this work, we combine a non-contact laser-induced transient thermal grating technique with ab initio phonon simulations to investigate the in-plane thermal transport of epitaxial GaAs-based buffer layers on Si, employed in the fabrication of III-V quantum dot lasers. Surprisingly, we find a significant reduction of the in-plane thermal conductivity of GaAs, up to 19%, as a result of a small in-plane biaxial stress of 250 MPa. Using ab initio phonon calculations, we attribute this effect to the enhancement of phonon-phonon scattering caused by the in-plane biaxial stress, which breaks the cubic crystal symmetry of GaAs. Our results indicate the importance of eliminating the residual thermal stress in the epitaxial III-V layers on Si to avoid the reduction of thermal conductivity and facilitate heat dissipation. Additionally, our results showcase potential means of effectively controlling thermal conductivity of solids with external strain/stress.

paper-1d5e1533af81dca2c7a6dc18a758534752.displayLabel: Effect of strain on the thermoelectric properties of silicon: an ab initio study

s2Metadata.title: Effect of strain on the thermoelectric properties of silicon: an ab initio study
s2Metadata.abstract: On the basis of detailed first-principles calculations the anisotropic thermoelectric transport properties of biaxially strained silicon were studied with the focus on a possible enhancement of the power factor. Electron as well as hole doping was examined in a broad doping and temperature range. In the low temperature and low doping regime an enhancement of the power factor was obtained for compressive and tensile strain in the electron-doped case, and for compressive strain in the hole-doped case. In the thermoelectrically more important high temperature and high doping regime a slight enhancement of the power factor was only found for the hole-doped case under small biaxial tensile strain. The results are discussed in terms of band structure effects. An analytical model is presented to understand the fact that the thermopower decreases if degenerate bands are energetically lifted due to a strain-induced redistribution of states.

paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db9.displayLabel: Experimental investigation of size effects on the thermal conductivity of silicon-germanium alloy thin films.

s2Metadata.title: Experimental investigation of size effects on the thermal conductivity of silicon-germanium alloy thin films.
s2Metadata.abstract: We experimentally investigate the role of size effects and boundary scattering on the thermal conductivity of silicon-germanium alloys. The thermal conductivities of a series of epitaxially grown Si(1-x)Ge(x) thin films with varying thicknesses and compositions were measured with time-domain thermoreflectance. The resulting conductivities are found to be 3 to 5 times less than bulk values and vary strongly with film thickness. By examining these measured thermal conductivities in the context of a previously established model, it is shown that long wavelength phonons, known to be the dominant heat carriers in alloy films, are strongly scattered by the film boundaries, thereby inducing the observed reductions in heat transport. These results are then generalized to silicon-germanium systems of various thicknesses and compositions; we find that the thermal conductivities of Si(1-x)Ge(x) superlattices are ultimately limited by finite size effects and sample size rather than periodicity or alloying. This demonstrates the strong influence of sample size in alloyed nanosystems. Therefore, if a comparison is to be made between the thermal conductivities of superlattices and alloys, the total sample thicknesses of each must be considered.

content.title: Coherent biaxial constraint implies tetragonal distortion and potential κ anisotropy

content.text: Coherent biaxial strain makes the lattice tetragonal, so phonon speeds (and thus thermal conductivity) can differ in-plane and cross-plane.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Epitaxial Ge on Si(001) is described as biaxially strained with tetragonal distortion confirmed by high-resolution XRD reciprocal-space maps; the analysis explicitly treats anisotropic (parallel vs perpendicular) thermal expansion under epitaxial constraint.  <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper>

- Ge1-xSnx layers grown on Ge/Si are likewise treated as tetragonally distorted biaxial epilayers under substrate/buffer constraint; Raman and XRD strains are compared and modeled with an anisotropic epitaxial-constraint framework.  <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.1">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper>

- A computational study applies biaxial in-plane strain to Si thin films and finds strain-tunable in-plane κ with mode-resolved changes in phonon properties, consistent with strain-induced alteration of phonon transport properties under biaxial constraint (though in a freestanding geometry).  <paper entityId="paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c637ebe" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="284077394" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Su et al., 2025</paper>

content.title: Directional κ change under biaxial strain is governed by velocity renormalization versus scattering renormalization

content.text: Strain changes thermal conductivity by changing phonon speeds and phonon lifetimes; direction-by-direction, whichever changes more determines whether κ goes up or down, and alloy scattering often makes the total change small.
**Supporting evidence:**

- The strained-Ge epilayer analysis extracts anisotropic Grüneisen parameters (γ∥, γ⊥) and an explicit anharmonic coefficient A3, indicating that epitaxial strain changes phonon frequency–strain response and explicit anharmonic renormalization parameters that would affect three-phonon scattering and thus τ.  <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper>

- For Ge/Si, A3 is larger in the epitaxial strained layer than in bulk Ge (A3 bulk ≈ 0.77 cm−1; A3 epilayer ≈ 1.0 cm−1), consistent with potentially stronger intrinsic anharmonic effects (shorter τ) in strained material, all else equal.  <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper>

- For GeSn epilayers, fitted γ values are similar (≈1.3) and A3 shows little dependence on composition and threading dislocation density, supporting the notion that changes in κ across similar alloys are more governed by disorder scattering than by large changes in intrinsic anharmonicity parameters.  <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.1">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper>

- The electronic-transport paper cites prior computational literature that tensile strain reduces κ in bulk Si (e.g., ~10% reduction at 3% isotropic tensile strain) and attributes reductions to reduced phonon group velocities and/or specific heat—consistent with the velocity/lifetime decomposition framework.  <paper entityId="paper-db50837f193e0e576acfdb1d75407a47f915daa6" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="119044537" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Vega-Flick et al., 2019</paper> <paper entityId="paper-1d5e1533af81dca2c7a6dc18a75853475238ef61" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="26897241" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.2">Hinsche et al., 2011</paper>

- The biaxially strained Si thin-film computational study explicitly computes mode-resolved group velocities and lifetimes and shows κ is strain-tunable, directly supporting the principle that κ changes can be decomposed into v and τ changes under biaxial strain (though for freestanding thin films).  <paper entityId="paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c637ebe" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="284077394" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Su et al., 2025</paper>

- Cheaito et al. show that in SiGe thin films, boundary scattering can dominate low-frequency heat-carrying phonons (size effects) and alloy scattering dominates high frequencies; this supports the special case that when extrinsic/boundary/alloy scattering caps τ, additional intrinsic strain-induced τ changes will have muted impact on κ magnitude.  <paper entityId="paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db949c821" annotationId="ann_010" corpusId="9397977" artifactId="extraction-result-12#uuid-e12.0">Cheaito et al., 2012</paper>

- This law/statement was logically inferred by combining the standard kinetic form κ ~ Σ C v^2 τ with evidence that (i) strain modifies phonon parameters linked to anharmonicity (γ, A3) and (ii) literature attributes strain effects to group-velocity/specific-heat changes; the directional form under biaxial strain is an anisotropic extension of these elements.

- For coherently compressed Si0.5Ge0.5 on Si(001) at 300 K, κ⊥ (cross-plane) will fall slightly relative to relaxed bulk (category: decrease), with a likely magnitude of ~5–12% decrease, while κ∥ increases modestly (few to ~10%) due to in-plane stiffening.
- For coherently strained Ge on Si(001), if one could isolate an otherwise defect-free epilayer, an increased A3 relative to bulk would correlate with reduced intrinsic τ and thus reduced κ compared with unstrained bulk at the same T, despite any stiffness-related v increases.
- In SiGe films where thickness/boundary scattering is already the shortest scattering time (as in Cheaito’s thin films), imposing additional coherent biaxial strain will change κ less (smaller |Δκ|) than in thicker, bulk-like samples at the same composition.

- A sign change with temperature for κ⊥ under coherent compression near x≈0.5: κ⊥ may decrease at 300 K but show weaker decrease or even slight increase at cryogenic temperatures if intrinsic three-phonon scattering becomes weak and velocity anisotropy dominates over strain-modified anharmonicity.
- At sufficiently large coherent biaxial strain (few percent) in SiGe, tetragonal splitting could nonlinearly increase three-phonon phase space for particular cross-plane polarized modes, producing a larger κ anisotropy than predicted by linear-elastic velocity changes alone.

- Perform spectral (mode-resolved) analysis for coherently strained Si0.5Ge0.5 and test whether strain changes (i) v∥ vs v⊥ and/or (ii) τ in a directionally correlated way; if neither v nor τ show meaningful anisotropy but κ does, the mechanism assignment is incomplete.
- Compare a coherently strained film to a plastically relaxed film of the same composition and thickness: if both show the same κ anisotropy, then coherence-induced tetragonal distortion is not the dominant cause (microstructure/interface effects would be implicated).
- In an alloy composition where τ is known to be alloy-scattering-limited, measure Δκ under strain; if Δκ is as large as in pure Si/Ge under comparable strain, then the 'alloy-scattering mutes strain response' component is falsified.

- Direct measurements or simulations of κ∥ and κ⊥ in coherently strained Si1-xGex (especially x=0.5) are not present in the provided evidence; therefore, magnitude calibration for the predicted percent changes remains uncertain.

content.title: Matthiessen-limited strain leverage on κ in alloy/thin-film regime

content.text: When alloy and boundary scattering already dominate, strain can only change thermal conductivity a little because lifetimes are already short.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Cheaito et al. model Si1-xGex thin films with Matthiessen’s rule combining Umklapp, alloy scattering τ_α = [x(1-x)A ω^4]^{-1}, and boundary scattering τ_b = d/v, and conclude boundary scattering of long-wavelength phonons dominates κ reductions in thin films; alloy scattering dominates at high frequencies.  <paper entityId="paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db949c821" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="9397977" artifactId="extraction-result-12#uuid-e12.0">Cheaito et al., 2012</paper>

- Cheaito et al. measure very low cross-plane κ in SiGe thin films (e.g., ~1.8–2.8 W/m-K for Si0.8Ge0.2 across 39–427 nm), illustrating that κ is already strongly suppressed by alloying/size compared with bulk, implying limited headroom for additional modest strain effects.  <paper entityId="paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db949c821" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="9397977" artifactId="extraction-result-12#uuid-e12.0">Cheaito et al., 2012</paper>

- Raman/XRD analysis of GeSn indicates A3 and γ show little dependence on composition or threading dislocation density in the studied range, supporting the idea that disorder/alloy scattering dominates κ variations rather than large strain-induced changes to intrinsic anharmonicity parameters.  <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.1">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper>

content.title: Thickness control can mask strain dependence in cross-plane κ measurements

content.text: If thickness is the main limiter of cross-plane heat flow, strain won’t change the measured cross-plane κ very much.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Cheaito et al. conclude boundary scattering of long-wavelength phonons dominates κ reductions in epitaxial SiGe thin films; their spectral analysis indicates τ_b is the shortest (limiting) for modes carrying most heat in the thinnest films.  <paper entityId="paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db949c821" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="9397977" artifactId="extraction-result-12#uuid-e12.0">Cheaito et al., 2012</paper>

- Cheaito et al. compare thin-film alloys and superlattices and argue total sample thickness controls κ similarly, consistent with size-limited scattering of long-wavelength phonons dominating over other mechanisms in many thin samples.  <paper entityId="paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db949c821" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="9397977" artifactId="extraction-result-12#uuid-e12.0">Cheaito et al., 2012</paper>

- For Si0.5Ge0.5 films where alloy scattering dominates, coherent biaxial strain of ~2% will change κ by at most low-teens percent at 300 K, even if anisotropic (κ∥ and κ⊥ can shift in opposite directions).
- If two SiGe films have the same thickness and composition but different coherent strain states (within the elastic stability range) and remain dislocation-free, κ differences will be smaller than differences caused by changing thickness by a factor of ~2 in the size-limited regime.
- In TDTR-style cross-plane measurements, the strain dependence of extracted κ⊥ will be weakest in the thinnest films (tens of nm), where τ_b dominates.

- In mid-alloy SiGe, sufficiently large coherent strain might shift the dominant heat-carrying spectrum toward frequencies where alloy scattering is weaker/stronger, producing a non-intuitive strain dependence (including potential nonmonotonic κ vs strain).
- If coherent strain significantly changes the acoustic–optical gap in SiGe alloys, it could alter the relative importance of Umklapp channels and amplify strain effects beyond the Matthiessen-limited expectation.

- If a mid-alloy SiGe film (x≈0.5) with strong alloy scattering exhibits a >30% κ change under modest coherent strain without introducing dislocations, this theory’s 'limited leverage' claim is falsified.
- If thinning a SiGe film does not reduce κ in the manner predicted by τ_b ≈ d/v dominance (holding composition constant), then the assumed dominance of boundary scattering for long-wavelength phonons is incorrect for that system.
- If mode-resolved analysis shows τ_U dominates over τ_alloy for the heat-carrying spectrum at x≈0.5 and 300 K, then intrinsic strain-induced changes to τ_U could be large and this theory’s hierarchy would not apply.
- The provided evidence does not include any direct strained/coherent Si0.5Ge0.5 κ data (in-plane or cross-plane) to numerically validate the magnitude bounds suggested here.

s2Metadata.title: Topological surface phonons modulate thermal transport in semiconductor thin films
s2Metadata.abstract: While phonon topology in crystalline solids has been extensively studied, its influence on thermal transport-especially in nanostructures-remains elusive. Here, by combining first-principles-based machine learning potentials with the phonon Boltzmann transport equation and molecular dynamics simulations, we systematically investigate the role of topological surface phonons in the in-plane thermal transport of semiconductor thin films (Si, 4H -SiC, and c-BN). These topological surface phonons, originating from nontrivial acoustic phonon nodal lines, not only serve as key scattering channels for dominant acoustic phonons but also contribute substantially to the overall thermal conductivity. Remarkably, for these thin semiconductor films below 10 nm this contribution can be as large as over 30% of the in-plane thermal conductivity at 300 K, and the largest absolute contribution can reach 82 W/m-K, highlighting their significant role in nanoscale thermal transport in semiconductors. content.title: Alloy-scattering dominance bounds intrinsic coherent-strain sensitivity of κ near x≈0.5

content.text: Near 50/50 SiGe, alloy disorder already limits heat flow, so coherent strain alone usually changes κ by only ~a few to ~10% unless it also creates defects or changes interface/boundary scattering.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Cheaito et al. model cross-plane κ of epitaxial Si1-xGex thin films using Matthiessen’s rule with an explicit alloy-scattering term τ_α^{-1} ∝ x(1−x)ω^4 and conclude that boundary scattering of long-wavelength phonons dominates thin-film reductions while alloy scattering remains an essential term (especially at higher frequencies). This supports that alloy scattering is a major baseline limiter in SiGe alloys and that additional perturbations (like strain) act on top of an already-strong scattering background.  <paper entityId="paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db949c821" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="9397977" artifactId="extraction-result-12#uuid-e12.0">Cheaito et al., 2012</paper>

- Cheaito et al. show that in thin films (39–427 nm) κ is already strongly suppressed (≈1.8–2.8 W/m·K for x=0.2) and that dislocation density trends with thickness do not straightforwardly explain κ trends, implying that boundary/alloy scattering dominate; this is consistent with a picture where moderate changes to intrinsic anharmonicity/velocities would yield only modest fractional changes in κ compared with dominant alloy/boundary limits.  <paper entityId="paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db949c821" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="9397977" artifactId="extraction-result-12#uuid-e12.0">Cheaito et al., 2012</paper>

- Raman/XRD analysis for epitaxial Ge/Si indicates the explicit anharmonic coefficient A3 is only slightly larger in epitaxial Ge/Si than bulk Ge (A3 bulk ≈0.77 cm−1 vs A3 Ge/Si ≈1.0 cm−1) and authors argue A3 is insensitive to large ranges of threading dislocation density and to alloying in related GeSn samples, suggesting that in similar group-IV alloys variations in κ are often more controlled by disorder/defect scattering than by strong shifts in intrinsic anharmonicity parameters.  <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper>

- The strained-Si electronic-transport paper notes (from literature) that tensile strain can reduce lattice κ by up to ~15% in bulk silicon and silicon thin films, providing a magnitude context that intrinsic strain leverage in a pure crystal is typically O(10%) even at sizeable strains; in a strong-scattering alloy, the fractional leverage is expected to be no larger and often smaller.  <paper entityId="paper-1d5e1533af81dca2c7a6dc18a75853475238ef61" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="26897241" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.0">Hinsche et al., 2011</paper>

- The same paper cites Parrish et al. as predicting ~10% κ reduction for bulk Si under 3% isotropic tensile strain, supporting the notion that even fairly large elastic deformations can yield only ~10% κ shifts when no new extrinsic scattering is introduced.  <paper entityId="paper-db50837f193e0e576acfdb1d75407a47f915daa6" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="119044537" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Vega-Flick et al., 2019</paper> <paper entityId="paper-1d5e1533af81dca2c7a6dc18a75853475238ef61" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="26897241" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.0">Hinsche et al., 2011</paper>

content.title: Anisotropic sign tendency under coherent biaxial compression on Si(001) for midrange SiGe

content.text: With coherent in-plane compression on Si, in-plane κ usually stays the same or rises a bit, while through-thickness κ usually stays the same or drops a bit, making κ more anisotropic.
**Supporting evidence:**

- The cited tensile-strain literature in the strained-Si electronic study (and its citations) indicates tensile strain reduces κ in Si by up to ~10–15%, commonly attributed to reduced phonon group velocities and/or modified harmonic properties. By inversion, compression tends to increase stiffness/velocities in the compressed directions, motivating Δκ∥≥0 under in-plane compression as a tendency.  <paper entityId="paper-1d5e1533af81dca2c7a6dc18a75853475238ef61" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="26897241" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.0">Hinsche et al., 2011</paper> <paper entityId="paper-db50837f193e0e576acfdb1d75407a47f915daa6" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="119044537" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Vega-Flick et al., 2019</paper>

- Epitaxial Ge/Si Raman/XRD analysis shows biaxial epitaxial constraint produces anisotropic Grüneisen parameters (γ∥ and γ⊥ reported) and modified anharmonic coefficient A3 relative to bulk, demonstrating that coherent biaxial strain can change anharmonic-related parameters and thus scattering in an anisotropic (tetragonal) fashion, supporting the mechanism that κ components can respond differently along ∥ and ⊥.  <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_009" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper>

- The biaxially strained Si thin-film computational study explicitly shows biaxial strain tunes in-plane κ through strain-driven changes in phonon group velocities and lifetimes (via PBTE with third-order IFCs), supporting the general causal link 'biaxial strain → changes in v and τ → changes in κ', even though those results are for ultrathin freestanding films and only in-plane κ.  <paper entityId="paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c637ebe" annotationId="ann_010" corpusId="284077394" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Su et al., 2025</paper>

- This law’s directional sign pattern for midrange SiGe under coherent compression is a synthesis/inference combining (i) tensile-strain κ reductions in Si (harmonic softening) and (ii) biaxial strain causing anisotropic phonon-parameter changes (γ, A3) in epitaxial group-IV films; direct SiGe strain-resolved κ data are not present in the provided evidence.

- H7 prediction (intrinsic lattice κ): For a coherently compressed Si0.5Ge0.5 film on Si(001) (~2% in-plane compression) at 300 K, cross-plane κ decreases relative to relaxed bulk Si0.5Ge0.5 by about 5–12% (nominal −8%); in-plane κ is unchanged to mildly increased (0 to +8%, nominal +3 to +5%).
- If the same Si0.5Ge0.5 alloy is simulated in a virtual-crystal (mass-disorder removed) but with the same coherent biaxial strain, the magnitude of strain-induced Δκ/κ will increase substantially (because τ becomes controlled more by strain-sensitive anharmonicity rather than alloy disorder).
- The anisotropy ratio κ∥/κ⊥ increases under coherent biaxial compression on Si(001) for x≈0.5, even if the average κ changes only weakly.

- There exists a composition window near x≈0.5 where cross-plane κ shows near-cancellation (|Δκ⊥|<5%) under ~2% coherent compression, while in-plane κ still increases measurably; this would imply unusually strong compensation between v⊥ and τ⊥ changes.
- If coherent strain biases local chemical environments (strain-coupled SRO) in Si0.5Ge0.5, alloy scattering may become correlation-dependent (deviating from simple x(1−x) scaling), amplifying Δκ/κ beyond the attenuation bound without introducing dislocations.

- In PBTE or spectral MD for coherently strained Si0.5Ge0.5, decompose κ into mode-resolved v^2 and τ: if strain changes τ by factors comparable to or larger than the baseline alloy scattering across heat-carrying modes at 300 K, the attenuation/bound claim is falsified.
- Prepare coherent vs relaxed Si0.5Ge0.5 samples with comparable thickness and defect densities (confirmed by XRD/TEM): if coherent biaxial strain alone systematically produces >25% changes in intrinsic κ⊥ at 300 K, the bounded-change statement fails.
- Compute κ for coherent strain but with artificially increased TDD/dislocation density: if κ changes remain small despite strong added defect scattering, then the model’s emphasis on extrinsic scattering as an override is incorrect.

- No direct strain-dependent κ data for coherently strained Si1-xGex are present in the provided evidence set; the theory relies on inferred scattering hierarchy (alloy/boundary) and strain–phonon-parameter sensitivity from related systems (strained Si, strained Ge).  <paper entityId="paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db949c821" annotationId="ann_011" corpusId="9397977" artifactId="extraction-result-12#uuid-e12.0">Cheaito et al., 2012</paper> <paper entityId="paper-1d5e1533af81dca2c7a6dc18a75853475238ef61" annotationId="ann_012" corpusId="26897241" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.0">Hinsche et al., 2011</paper> <paper entityId="paper-db50837f193e0e576acfdb1d75407a47f915daa6" annotationId="ann_013" corpusId="119044537" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Vega-Flick et al., 2019</paper> <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_014" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper>

s2Metadata.title:
Thermal expansion and temperature dependence of Raman modes in epitaxial layers of Ge and 
<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>Ge</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mtext>−</mml:mtext><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mi>Sn<
s2Metadata.abstract: Temperature dependence of vibrational modes in semiconductors depends on lattice thermal expansion and anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering. Evaluating the two contributions from experimental data is not straightforward, especially for epitaxial layers that present mechanical deformation and anisotropic lattice expansion. In this work, a temperature-dependent Raman study in epitaxial Ge and Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$ layers is presented. A model is introduced for the Raman mode energy shift as a function of temperature, comprising thermal expansion of the strained lattice and anharmonic corrections. With support of x-ray diffraction, the model is calibrated on experimental data of epitaxial Ge grown on Si and Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$ grown on Ge/Si, finding that the main difference between bulk and epitaxial layers is related to the anisotropic lattice expansion. The phonon anharmonicity and other parameters do not depend on dislocation defect density (in the range $7\cdot 10^6$ - $4\cdot 10^8$ cm$^{-2}$) nor on alloy composition in the range 5-14 at.%. The strain-shift coefficient for the main model of Ge and for the Ge-Ge vibrational mode of Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$ is weakly dependent on temperature and is around -500 cm$^{-1}$. In Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$, the composition-shift coefficient amounts to -100 cm$^{-1}$, independent of temperature and strain.

content.title: Cubic-to-tetragonal symmetry breaking splits modes and alters three-phonon phase space anisotropically

content.text: Making the lattice tetragonal by biaxial strain changes which phonons can scatter, and that effect is direction-dependent.
**Supporting evidence:**

- The biaxially strained Si thin-film PBTE study computes mode-resolved weighted phase space (WPS) and lifetimes and shows that biaxial strain tunes κ through changes in velocities and scattering phase space/lifetimes (even if reported primarily for in-plane κ).  <paper entityId="paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c637ebe" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="284077394" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Su et al., 2025</paper>

- Epitaxial Ge/Si Raman/XRD analysis extracts anisotropic Grüneisen parameters (γ∥, γ⊥) under biaxial constraint, evidencing anisotropic phonon-strain coupling consistent with tetragonal symmetry breaking affecting phonon properties relevant to scattering.  <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper>

- For coherently strained SiGe, the anisotropy κ∥/κ⊥ will increase with |ε∥| even when the average κ changes weakly, because WPS changes are anisotropic under tetragonal distortion.
- Mode-resolved PBTE for strained Si0.5Ge0.5 will show larger relative lifetime changes for subsets of acoustic modes with polarization aligned to the strain-relaxed direction (out-of-plane) than for purely in-plane polarized modes.

- There exists a strain magnitude at which avoided crossings induced by tetragonal splitting create a sharp change in WPS for a narrow frequency window, producing a nonmonotonic κ⊥(ε∥) even in relatively thick films.
- In SiGe, tetragonal strain may shift the balance between Normal and Umklapp processes differently for ∥ and ⊥ heat flux, leading to different hydrodynamic-like signatures (second sound windows) in-plane vs cross-plane at intermediate temperatures.

- Compute strained vs unstrained Si0.5Ge0.5 PBTE and explicitly compare WPS(ω) and matrix elements: if WPS changes are negligible while κ anisotropy changes substantially, the phase-space mechanism is insufficient.
- If κ anisotropy changes track only elastic constants/sound speeds with no additional lifetime anisotropy, then the symmetry-driven scattering-channel reshaping is not a primary mechanism.

- No direct κ∥ and κ⊥ data under coherent biaxial strain in SiGe are provided; evidence is indirect via Raman-derived parameters in Ge and PBTE thin-film Si results.  <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper> <paper entityId="paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c637ebe" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="284077394" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Su et al., 2025</paper>

paper-db50837f193e0e576acfdb1d75407a47f9.displayLabel: Reduced thermal conductivity of epitaxial GaAs on Si due to symmetry-breaking biaxial strain

s2Metadata.title: Reduced thermal conductivity of epitaxial GaAs on Si due to symmetry-breaking biaxial strain
s2Metadata.abstract: Epitaxial growth of III-V semiconductors on Si is a promising route for silicon photonics. Threading dislocations and the residual thermal stress generated during growth are expected to affect the thermal conductivity of the III-V semiconductors, which is crucial for efficient heat dissipation from photonic devices built on this platform. In this work, we combine a non-contact laser-induced transient thermal grating technique with ab initio phonon simulations to investigate the in-plane thermal transport of epitaxial GaAs-based buffer layers on Si, employed in the fabrication of III-V quantum dot lasers. Surprisingly, we find a significant reduction of the in-plane thermal conductivity of GaAs, up to 19%, as a result of a small in-plane biaxial stress of 250 MPa. Using ab initio phonon calculations, we attribute this effect to the enhancement of phonon-phonon scattering caused by the in-plane biaxial stress, which breaks the cubic crystal symmetry of GaAs. Our results indicate the importance of eliminating the residual thermal stress in the epitaxial III-V layers on Si to avoid the reduction of thermal conductivity and facilitate heat dissipation. Additionally, our results showcase potential means of effectively controlling thermal conductivity of solids with external strain/stress.

paper-1d5e1533af81dca2c7a6dc18a758534752.displayLabel: Effect of strain on the thermoelectric properties of silicon: an ab initio study

s2Metadata.title: Effect of strain on the thermoelectric properties of silicon: an ab initio study
s2Metadata.abstract: On the basis of detailed first-principles calculations the anisotropic thermoelectric transport properties of biaxially strained silicon were studied with the focus on a possible enhancement of the power factor. Electron as well as hole doping was examined in a broad doping and temperature range. In the low temperature and low doping regime an enhancement of the power factor was obtained for compressive and tensile strain in the electron-doped case, and for compressive strain in the hole-doped case. In the thermoelectrically more important high temperature and high doping regime a slight enhancement of the power factor was only found for the hole-doped case under small biaxial tensile strain. The results are discussed in terms of band structure effects. An analytical model is presented to understand the fact that the thermopower decreases if degenerate bands are energetically lifted due to a strain-induced redistribution of states.

paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db9.displayLabel: Experimental investigation of size effects on the thermal conductivity of silicon-germanium alloy thin films.

s2Metadata.title: Experimental investigation of size effects on the thermal conductivity of silicon-germanium alloy thin films.
s2Metadata.abstract: We experimentally investigate the role of size effects and boundary scattering on the thermal conductivity of silicon-germanium alloys. The thermal conductivities of a series of epitaxially grown Si(1-x)Ge(x) thin films with varying thicknesses and compositions were measured with time-domain thermoreflectance. The resulting conductivities are found to be 3 to 5 times less than bulk values and vary strongly with film thickness. By examining these measured thermal conductivities in the context of a previously established model, it is shown that long wavelength phonons, known to be the dominant heat carriers in alloy films, are strongly scattered by the film boundaries, thereby inducing the observed reductions in heat transport. These results are then generalized to silicon-germanium systems of various thicknesses and compositions; we find that the thermal conductivities of Si(1-x)Ge(x) superlattices are ultimately limited by finite size effects and sample size rather than periodicity or alloying. This demonstrates the strong influence of sample size in alloyed nanosystems. Therefore, if a comparison is to be made between the thermal conductivities of superlattices and alloys, the total sample thicknesses of each must be considered.

content.title: Tetragonal distortion induces directional sound-speed changes that bias κ|| vs κ⊥

content.text: Biaxial strain makes phonon speeds different in-plane vs out-of-plane, so κ becomes anisotropic because κ scales like speed-squared times lifetime.
**Supporting evidence:**

- The strain state in epitaxial (001) group-IV layers is explicitly described as biaxial/tetragonal distortion under substrate constraint (epilayer thermal expansion anisotropic; a|| constrained).  <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper>

- Prior isotropic tensile-strain predictions cited in the provided materials attribute κ reductions mainly to reduced phonon group velocities and/or specific heat (harmonic-property changes).  <paper entityId="paper-db50837f193e0e576acfdb1d75407a47f915daa6" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="119044537" artifactId="extraction-result-7#uuid-e7.0">Vega-Flick et al., 2019</paper> <paper entityId="paper-1d5e1533af81dca2c7a6dc18a75853475238ef61" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="26897241" artifactId="extraction-result-10#uuid-e10.2">Hinsche et al., 2011</paper>

- In strained Si thin-film PBTE/HNEMD work, biaxial strain modulates phonon dispersions and group velocities (mode-resolved velocities computed) and tunes in-plane κ, demonstrating that strain-driven dispersion/velocity changes can control κ in group-IV Si systems.  <paper entityId="paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c637ebe" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="284077394" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Su et al., 2025</paper>

content.title: Alloy/boundary dominated regimes suppress κ sensitivity to modest anharmonic-parameter shifts

content.text: If alloy disorder or film thickness already limits phonon lifetimes, changing intrinsic anharmonicity a bit won’t move κ much; velocities and extrinsic scattering matter more.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Measured cross-plane κ of epitaxial Si1−xGex films is strongly reduced relative to bulk and is explained by a model dominated by boundary scattering of long-wavelength phonons (τb = d/v) plus alloy scattering (∝ ω^4) and Umklapp; authors conclude boundary scattering dominates reductions in thin films.  <paper entityId="paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db949c821" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="9397977" artifactId="extraction-result-12#uuid-e12.0">Cheaito et al., 2012</paper>

- Raman/XRD study concludes A3 (anharmonic coefficient) is relatively insensitive to TDD and modest alloying; authors infer disorder/alloy scattering likely dominates κ variations rather than changes in anharmonicity in similar systems.  <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper>

- Thin-film Si under biaxial strain shows κ tunability linked to strain-modulated surface states/reconstructions, highlighting a special-case mechanism beyond bulk anharmonic renormalization.  <paper entityId="paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c637ebe" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="284077394" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Su et al., 2025</paper>

- For coherently strained Si0.5Ge0.5 on Si(001) (~2% in-plane compression), the cross-plane κ change at 300 K will be modest (within ~±10%) because alloy and film-size scattering dominate, unless strain significantly modifies low-frequency acoustic dispersion; κ anisotropy (κ|| ≠ κ⊥) will increase relative to relaxed bulk.
- In a Debye/RTA fit of strained vs unstrained SiGe film data at fixed thickness, the best-fit change needed to match κ shifts will mainly appear as a change in effective sound speeds (v||, v⊥) rather than large changes in Umklapp prefactors.

- At x≈0.5, biaxial strain may push an acoustic-optical avoided crossing to lower frequency, sharply increasing three-phonon phase space and causing an unexpectedly large κ⊥ drop (>15%) even in an alloy-dominated regime.
- If coherent strain modifies local short-range order tendencies in SiGe (not included in simple alloy models), κ may change more strongly than predicted by purely harmonic anisotropy.

- PBTE with strain-dependent 3rd-order IFCs for Si0.5Ge0.5: if τU changes by >20% at 2% biaxial strain while v changes are small, then the theory’s emphasis on harmonic anisotropy/extrinsic dominance fails for this composition.
- MD or PBTE separating κ|| and κ⊥: if κ remains isotropic under tetragonal distortion in a defect-free coherent cell, then the claimed inevitable κ anisotropy from v||≠v⊥ is incorrect.

- No direct experimental κ measurements for coherently strained Ge/Si or GeSn/Ge/Si are provided; evidence links strain to phonon parameter shifts (γ, A3) but not to measured κ.  <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper>

paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db9.displayLabel: Experimental investigation of size effects on the thermal conductivity of silicon-germanium alloy thin films.

s2Metadata.title: Experimental investigation of size effects on the thermal conductivity of silicon-germanium alloy thin films.
s2Metadata.abstract: We experimentally investigate the role of size effects and boundary scattering on the thermal conductivity of silicon-germanium alloys. The thermal conductivities of a series of epitaxially grown Si(1-x)Ge(x) thin films with varying thicknesses and compositions were measured with time-domain thermoreflectance. The resulting conductivities are found to be 3 to 5 times less than bulk values and vary strongly with film thickness. By examining these measured thermal conductivities in the context of a previously established model, it is shown that long wavelength phonons, known to be the dominant heat carriers in alloy films, are strongly scattered by the film boundaries, thereby inducing the observed reductions in heat transport. These results are then generalized to silicon-germanium systems of various thicknesses and compositions; we find that the thermal conductivities of Si(1-x)Ge(x) superlattices are ultimately limited by finite size effects and sample size rather than periodicity or alloying. This demonstrates the strong influence of sample size in alloyed nanosystems. Therefore, if a comparison is to be made between the thermal conductivities of superlattices and alloys, the total sample thicknesses of each must be considered.

Thermal expansion and temperature dependence of Raman modes in epitaxial layers of Ge and 
<mml:math xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mml:mrow><mml:msub><mml:mi>Ge</mml:mi><mml:mrow><mml:mn>1</mml:mn><mml:mtext>−</mml:mtext><mml:mi>x</mml:mi></mml:mrow></mml:msub><mml:msub><mml:mi>Sn<
s2Metadata.abstract: Temperature dependence of vibrational modes in semiconductors depends on lattice thermal expansion and anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering. Evaluating the two contributions from experimental data is not straightforward, especially for epitaxial layers that present mechanical deformation and anisotropic lattice expansion. In this work, a temperature-dependent Raman study in epitaxial Ge and Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$ layers is presented. A model is introduced for the Raman mode energy shift as a function of temperature, comprising thermal expansion of the strained lattice and anharmonic corrections. With support of x-ray diffraction, the model is calibrated on experimental data of epitaxial Ge grown on Si and Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$ grown on Ge/Si, finding that the main difference between bulk and epitaxial layers is related to the anisotropic lattice expansion. The phonon anharmonicity and other parameters do not depend on dislocation defect density (in the range $7\cdot 10^6$ - $4\cdot 10^8$ cm$^{-2}$) nor on alloy composition in the range 5-14 at.%. The strain-shift coefficient for the main model of Ge and for the Ge-Ge vibrational mode of Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$ is weakly dependent on temperature and is around -500 cm$^{-1}$. In Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_{x}$, the composition-shift coefficient amounts to -100 cm$^{-1}$, independent of temperature and strain.

content.title: Boundary filtering sets a strain-sensitive spectral window for κ in thin SiGe

content.text: Thickness pushes heat conduction to different phonon frequencies; strain matters most when those frequencies sit near where scattering mechanisms switch dominance.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Cheaito et al. model uses τb=d/v and concludes boundary scattering of long-wavelength phonons dominates κ reduction in thin SiGe films; spectral integrand peak shifts with thickness (lower frequency for thicker films, higher frequency for thinner films).  <paper entityId="paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db949c821" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="9397977" artifactId="extraction-result-12#uuid-e12.0">Cheaito et al., 2012</paper>

content.title: Alloy scattering attenuates strain-driven κ changes at x≈0.5 by shortening τ across much of the spectrum

content.text: At around 50% alloying, disorder scattering is so strong that small strain effects are usually muted, except possibly for the very low-frequency modes.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Cheaito et al. explicitly includes alloy scattering τa=[x(1−x)Aω^4]−1 in a Matthiessen model and finds thin-film κ is only weakly dependent on composition across broad x ranges compared to bulk, consistent with strong extrinsic limitations.  <paper entityId="paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db949c821" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="9397977" artifactId="extraction-result-12#uuid-e12.0">Cheaito et al., 2012</paper>

- Ge/Si and GeSn/Ge/Si Raman/XRD analysis suggests thermal-conductivity variations in similar alloys are more controlled by alloy/disorder scattering than by changes in anharmonic coefficient A3.  <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper>

- If the same Si0.5Ge0.5 film is simulated at multiple thicknesses under the same coherent biaxial strain, the percent change in κ with strain will be thickness-dependent, peaking at an intermediate thickness where the κ integrand peak lies near the boundary/alloy crossover.
- For a fixed thickness, strain will change κ more at lower temperatures (e.g., 150–250 K) than at 300–400 K if boundary filtering makes the contribution more sensitive to small dispersion shifts (while Umklapp grows at high T).

- A small strain (≈2%) could shift the spectral peak enough to change which branch dominates (LA vs TA) in the filtered spectrum, flipping the sign of the strain-induced κ change as thickness varies.
- If coherent strain modifies phonon localization tendencies in random SiGe (e.g., via strain-induced force-constant disorder amplification), κ could drop sharply beyond what ω^4 alloy scattering predicts.

- Mode-resolved PBTE for strained/unstrained Si0.5Ge0.5 at fixed thickness: if the κ spectral integrand peak does not shift with thickness as in Cheaito-like trends, the boundary-filtering premise is wrong for the simulation conditions/potential.
- If κ strain sensitivity is independent of thickness over a wide thickness range, the proposed crossover-controlled sensitivity mechanism is falsified.

- The evidence base does not contain direct measurements/simulations of strain-dependent κ in SiGe alloys; it only contains unstrained thin-film κ and strain-sensitive phonon parameters in Ge/GeSn.  <paper entityId="paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db949c821" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="9397977" artifactId="extraction-result-12#uuid-e12.0">Cheaito et al., 2012</paper> <paper entityId="paper-78d2f950c316e7e722c26b3de5ba860128a7dcfb" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="267413189" artifactId="extraction-result-9#uuid-e9.0">Corley-Wiciak et al., 2024</paper>

paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c.displayLabel: Topological surface phonons modulate thermal transport in semiconductor thin films

s2Metadata.title: Topological surface phonons modulate thermal transport in semiconductor thin films
s2Metadata.abstract: While phonon topology in crystalline solids has been extensively studied, its influence on thermal transport-especially in nanostructures-remains elusive. Here, by combining first-principles-based machine learning potentials with the phonon Boltzmann transport equation and molecular dynamics simulations, we systematically investigate the role of topological surface phonons in the in-plane thermal transport of semiconductor thin films (Si, 4H -SiC, and c-BN). These topological surface phonons, originating from nontrivial acoustic phonon nodal lines, not only serve as key scattering channels for dominant acoustic phonons but also contribute substantially to the overall thermal conductivity. Remarkably, for these thin semiconductor films below 10 nm this contribution can be as large as over 30% of the in-plane thermal conductivity at 300 K, and the largest absolute contribution can reach 82 W/m-K, highlighting their significant role in nanoscale thermal transport in semiconductors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that both temperature and biaxial strain provide effective means to modulate this contribution. Our work establishes a direct link between topological surface phonons and nanoscale thermal transport, offering the first quantitative assessment of their role and paving the way for topology-enabled thermal management in semiconductors.

content.title: Surface-phonon fraction controls strain sensitivity in ultrathin Si

content.text: In a few-nanometer Si membrane, surface phonons carry a big share of heat, and strain changes them, so κ can change a lot and not necessarily in one direction.
**Supporting evidence:**

- Mode-resolved PBTE/HNEMD results for Si thin films show that topological-surface-state-dominated phonons contribute ≥20% for Si(001) films when thickness t < 3.02 nm and ≥30% for Si(111) films when t < 4.5 nm, indicating a large surface-mode fraction in the ultrathin regime.  <paper entityId="paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c637ebe" annotationId="ann_001" corpusId="284077394" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Su et al., 2025</paper>

- The same study reports biaxial strain from −3% to +3% tunes in-plane κ and shows nonmonotonic behavior (reported explicitly for Si(111) a-type in strain-dependent plots), attributing strain sensitivity primarily to strain-driven changes in surface reconstruction and corresponding modulation of low-frequency surface phonon states.  <paper entityId="paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c637ebe" annotationId="ann_002" corpusId="284077394" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Su et al., 2025</paper>

- Mode-resolved quantities (group velocities, lifetimes, weighted phase space) are computed and presented for ~3 nm films, supporting the premise that certain low-frequency surface-dominated modes can have relatively large group velocities and long lifetimes and thus substantial κ contribution.  <paper entityId="paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c637ebe" annotationId="ann_003" corpusId="284077394" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Su et al., 2025</paper>

- The computational setup uses free surfaces in cross-plane direction with reconstructions (not substrate interfaces), consistent with the domain where surface-mode physics can dominate strain response.  <paper entityId="paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c637ebe" annotationId="ann_004" corpusId="284077394" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Su et al., 2025</paper>

content.title: Nonmonotonic κ(ε) as a diagnostic fingerprint of surface-reconstruction-controlled transport

content.text: If κ changes nonmonotonically with strain and depends strongly on surface structure, surface phonons are likely controlling heat flow; if not, bulk-like phonons and other scattering dominate.
**Supporting evidence:**

- The thin-film Si study explicitly attributes strain sensitivity primarily to strain-driven changes in surface reconstruction and modulation of low-frequency surface phonon states rather than a simple bulk stiffening/softening picture.  <paper entityId="paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c637ebe" annotationId="ann_005" corpusId="284077394" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Su et al., 2025</paper>

- Observed strain dependence includes nonmonotonic behavior of surface-mode contribution (reported for Si(111) as strain varies −3% to +3%), consistent with using nonmonotonicity as a fingerprint of reconstruction-controlled transport.  <paper entityId="paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c637ebe" annotationId="ann_006" corpusId="284077394" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Su et al., 2025</paper>

- The study provides mode-resolved group velocities/lifetimes/WPS, supporting the mechanism that strain can change scattering phase space and modal participation rather than only changing an average sound speed.  <paper entityId="paper-3a18285b8e5424631e9b23c23936dc073c637ebe" annotationId="ann_007" corpusId="284077394" artifactId="extraction-result-8#uuid-e8.0">Su et al., 2025</paper>

- Capping an ultrathin (≈2–4 nm) strained Si membrane with an amorphous layer or chemically terminating the surface to suppress reconstruction should substantially reduce both (i) the magnitude of strain tunability of in-plane κ and (ii) any nonmonotonic κ(ε) behavior; κ(ε) should become more monotonic and weaker.
- At fixed thickness in the ultrathin regime, surfaces/orientations with larger reported surface-mode κ fractions (e.g., Si(111) vs some Si(001) cases in the cited study) should exhibit larger strain tunability and a higher likelihood of nonmonotonic κ(ε) under similar biaxial strain sweeps.
- In simulations, if surface reconstruction is artificially constrained (atoms fixed to an unstrained reconstructed pattern while applying strain), the strain dependence of κ should be reduced compared to fully relaxed surfaces, indicating reconstruction as the primary mediator.

- A substrate-supported but ultrathin Si film with one free reconstructed top surface and one clamped bottom interface could show a mixed response: nonmonotonic strain dependence in in-plane κ from the free surface, but reduced amplitude compared to a fully freestanding membrane; the sign and strength would depend sensitively on interface bonding and whether the substrate damps surface-localized modes.
- In SiGe ultrathin membranes (few nm) with free surfaces, there may be a crossover where alloy disorder suppresses surface-mode channeling enough that κ(ε) becomes monotonic; identifying the critical Ge fraction for this crossover could reveal an interaction between surface-mode physics and mass-disorder scattering.

- If a 2–3 nm freestanding Si membrane with reconstructed surfaces shows strictly monotonic in-plane κ versus biaxial strain over −3% to +3% and negligible dependence on surface termination/reconstruction, then the proposed surface-reconstruction control mechanism is incomplete or not dominant.
- If mode-resolved decomposition in the ultrathin regime finds surface-localized/topological-surface-state-dominated modes contribute <5% of in-plane κ (contradicting the reported order-tens-of-percent), then the central premise of surface-mode channeling fails for that system/conditions.
- If modifying surface reconstruction (e.g., by controlled passivation) changes κ at zero strain but does not change κ(ε) trends, then nonmonotonic strain dependence would require an alternative mechanism (e.g., purely bulk-like dispersion/lifetime changes).

- This theory does not address cross-plane thermal conductivity or strain response in thick, substrate-clamped epitaxial SiGe films (e.g., Si0.5Ge0.5 coherently grown on Si) where alloy scattering and epitaxial constraint dominate; it is intentionally specialized to freestanding/free-surface ultrathin Si membranes.

- Through-thickness TDTR data on epitaxial Si1-xGex films emphasizing boundary scattering and thickness effects (rather than explicit strain effects) are outside this theory’s scope.  <paper entityId="paper-f4b61e79046c6358a8e34f944e1e7e3db949c821" annotationId="ann_008" corpusId="9397977" artifactId="extraction-result-12#uuid-e12.0">Cheaito et al., 2012</paper>
